entities.name: Alice
entities.description:
Alice, a curious, talkative young girl who falls down a rabbit-hole into a strange underground world, where she repeatedly grows and shrinks, and who wakes at the end on the riverbank beside her sister.

Personality:
- Curious and burning with curiosity; thinks it is not so very much out of the way to hear a rabbit speak.
- Impulsive: ran across the field after the White Rabbit and followed it down a rabbit-hole, never once considering how she was to get out again.
- Wise and cautious: will not drink from a bottle in a hurry, and says "No, I'll look first" to check for "poison".
- Has read histories about children who came to harm by ignoring simple rules, and never forgot that much from a bottle marked "poison" is almost certain to disagree with you.
- Likes to show off her schoolroom knowledge, even with no one to listen.
- Kind to her feet; plans to give them a new pair of boots every Christmas.
- Good-natured and helpful: always ready to make herself useful, looks anxiously about her, offers to help undo a knot, and good-naturedly hunts for the fan and gloves.
- Courageous and sometimes bold: surprised at her own courage; not afraid of the playing cards.
- Dislikes being ordered about, and grows impatient with the creatures' rudeness and riddles.
- Polite and timid when addressing creatures in authority, but sharp and scolding toward herself.
- Gets upset and cries easily, and her tears form a pool.
- Tends toward pride in her manners and knowledge, and is a little irritated by short or rude answers.
- Feels she has got so much into the way of expecting out-of-the-way things that ordinary life seems dull and stupid to her.
- Very fond of pretending to be two people, and generally gives herself very good advice, though she seldom follows it.
- Doubts that she is herself and is puzzled by her own identity.

Wants:
- To get out of the dark hall and into the lovely garden among the beds of bright flowers and cool fountains; does not care which happens to get there.
- To find a way to shut up like a telescope, or to find a key or a book of rules for shutting people up like telescopes.
- To grow back to her right size and then find her way into the lovely garden.
- To get out of the room where she is stuck after growing too large, and to be pulled out of the window.
- To find out who she is, and to know whether she was changed in the night.
- To go home, and to have Dinah the cat with her.
- To have someone to talk to.
- To get dry, as she is sure she will catch a bad cold otherwise.
- To change the subject whenever a conversation turns unpleasant, and to avoid offending creatures again.
- To escape the Queen and the court, and to be safe from being beheaded.
- To stop being ordered about by mice, rabbits and others.

Knows:
- She fell down a very deep well, falling very slowly with plenty of time to look about her.
- She tried to look down to see what she was coming to, but it was too dark to see anything.
- She took a jar labelled 'ORANGE MARMALADE' from a shelf as she passed and put it into a cupboard as she fell past it, because she did not want to drop it for fear of killing somebody underneath.
- She thinks that after such a fall she will think nothing of tumbling down stairs, and that people at home will think her brave.
- She says she would not say anything about it even if she fell off the top of the house, which she notes is very likely true.
- She asks aloud how many miles she has fallen and believes she must be getting somewhere near the centre of the earth, estimating four thousand miles down.
- She wonders what Latitude or Longitude she has got to; she has no idea what they are, but thinks they are nice grand words to say.
- She wonders whether she will fall right through the earth and come out among the Antipathies, people who walk with their heads downward.
- She thinks she would have to ask them the name of the country, and asks whether it is New Zealand or Australia.
- She tried to curtsey while falling.
- She thinks she would seem an ignorant little girl for asking, so she decides not to ask and hopes to see it written up somewhere.
- She misses Dinah, her cat, wishes Dinah were with her, and asks whether cats eat bats.
- She dozed off and dreamed she was walking hand in hand with Dinah, asking whether Dinah ever ate a bat.
- She landed with a thump upon a heap of sticks and dry leaves, and the fall was over.
- She was not hurt, and jumped up to her feet in a moment.
- She walked sadly down the middle of the hall wondering how she was ever to get out again.
- She was just in time to hear the White Rabbit say "Oh my ears and whiskers, how late it's getting!" as it turned a corner.
- She found the little golden key fitted the lock of the little door, to her great delight; her first thought was that the tiny golden key might belong to one of the doors of the hall.
- She has had many out-of-the-way things happen to her lately, so she has begun to think that very few things are really impossible.
- She has read several nice little histories about children who got burnt, eaten by wild beasts, or otherwise harmed.
- She wishes she could shut up like a telescope and thinks she could if she only knew how to begin.
- She went back to the table hoping to find another key on it.
- She ventured to taste the bottle and finished it off.
- After drinking, she felt she was shutting up like a telescope and was now only ten inches high.
- Her face brightened at the thought that she was now the right size for going through the little door into the lovely garden.
- She felt a little nervous about shrinking further, worrying it might end "in my going out altogether, like a candle".
- She could not remember ever having seen the flame of a candle after it was blown out.
- She forgot the little golden key, could not reach it, tried to climb one of the legs of the table but it was too slippery, and tired herself out, sat down and cried.
- She once remembered trying to box her own ears for having cheated herself in a game of croquet she was playing against herself.
- She opened the little glass box, found a very small cake marked "EAT ME", and ate a little bit of it, holding her hand on the top of her head to feel which way she was growing.
- She was quite surprised to find that she remained the same size.
- She set to work and very soon finished off the cake.
- She grew enormously tall, to more than nine feet high, and was so surprised she forgot how to speak good English for the moment.
- She is crying and shedding gallons of tears, creating a large pool around her about four inches deep and reaching half down the hall.
- She took up the little golden key and hurried off to the garden door, but found getting through hopeless.
- After a time she hastily dried her eyes to see what was coming; she felt so desperate that she was ready to ask help of anyone.
- As the hall was very hot, she kept fanning herself with the fan all the time she went on talking.
- She wonders if she has been changed in the night; she thinks she almost can remember feeling a little different this morning.
- She began thinking over all the children she knew who were of the same age as herself, to see if she could have been changed for any of them.
- She doubts she is Ada because her hair does not go in long ringlets as Ada's does.
- She doubts she is Mabel because she knows all sorts of things and Mabel knows such a very little.
- She tried to test her knowledge: "four times five is twelve", "four times six is thirteen", "London is the capital of Paris, and Paris is the capital of Rome", and concluded "that's all wrong" and "I must have been changed for Mabel!"
- She tried to recite "How doth the little crocodile", but her voice sounded hoarse and strange and the words did not come the same as they used to.
- If she is Mabel, she would have to go and live in that poky little house with next to no toys and many lessons to learn, so she decides she will stay down here.
- She says people putting their heads down and saying "Come up again, dear!" would be no use; she will only ask "Who am I then? Tell me that first".
- She put on one of the Rabbit's little white kid gloves without noticing, and then measured herself against the table and found she was about two feet high and still shrinking rapidly.
- She soon found the cause was the fan she was holding, so she dropped it hastily just in time to avoid shrinking away altogether.
- She ran back to the little door, but it was shut again, and the little golden key was lying on the glass table as before.
- Her foot slipped and she fell splash into salt water up to her chin.
- She first thought she had fallen into the sea and said she could then go back by railway.
- She has been to the seaside once in her life; she has come to the general conclusion that on the English coast you find bathing machines in the sea, children digging in the sand with wooden spades, a row of lodging houses, and behind them a railway station.
- She made out that she was in the pool of tears she had wept when she was nine feet high.
- She knows the French sentence "Où est ma chatte?", the first sentence in her French lesson-book.
- She remembered seeing "A mouse—of a mouse—to a mouse—a mouse—O mouse!" in her brother's Latin Grammar.
- She has knowledge of history but no very clear notion how long ago anything had happened.
- She wishes she could show the Mouse her cat Dinah, and believes the Mouse would take a fancy to cats if she could see Dinah.
- She wants to show the Mouse a nice little dog near her house.
- She led the way when the party swam to the shore.
- She talked familiarly with the birds and animals as if she had known them all her life.
- She had a long argument with the Lory about its age, and would not allow the Lory's claim to be older without knowing how old it was.
- She kept her eyes anxiously fixed on the Mouse while sitting in the ring.
- She does not know what a Caucus-race is, though she did not especially want to know.
- She had no idea what to do when the party demanded prizes; in despair she put her hand in her pocket and pulled out a box of comfits (the salt water had not got into it), and handed them round, giving exactly one apiece, all round.
- She has only a thimble in her pocket, which she describes sadly.
- She thought the thimble presentation very absurd, but did not dare to laugh because they all looked so grave; she simply bowed and took the thimble, looking as solemn as she could.
- She asked the Mouse to tell its history, as it had promised, and asked why it hates C and D.
- She wondered at the Mouse's tail and asked why it is called sad.
- She was severely reprimanded by the Mouse for not attending.
- She wishes she had Dinah here to fetch the Mouse back; Dinah is "such a capital one for catching mice".
- She was left alone after the birds moved off, felt very lonely and low-spirited, and began to cry.
- She wishes she hadn't mentioned Dinah; she believes Dinah is the best cat in the world and wonders if she will ever see her again.
- She felt everything had changed since her swim in the pool.
- She went hunting about and was noticed by the Rabbit, who pointed her toward the house; she was so frightened that she ran off at once in the direction it pointed, without explaining the mistake.
- She intends to take the Rabbit his fan and gloves, if she can find them.
- She thinks it is queer to be going messages for a rabbit, and imagines Dinah will be sending her on messages next.
- She imagines being called by nurse to get ready for a walk while she watches the mouse.
- She doubts they would let Dinah stay in the house if it began ordering people about like that.
- She takes up the fan and a pair of tiny white kid gloves.
- She drank from the little magic bottle to see what it would do, hoping it would make her grow large again, as she is quite tired of being such a tiny little thing.
- The bottle made her grow much larger than she expected: her head pressed against the ceiling, she had to stoop to save her neck from breaking, then kneel and lie down on the floor, with one elbow against the door and her other arm curled round her head.
- As a last resource she put one arm out of the window and one foot up the chimney, saying "Now I can do no more, whatever happens. What will become of me?"
- She says she wishes she had not drunk so much.
- The bottle's magic then stopped, and she grew no larger; she is very uncomfortable and unhappy, because there seems to be no chance of getting out of the room again.
- She thinks it was much pleasanter at home.
- She almost wishes she had not gone down the rabbit-hole, yet finds this sort of life rather curious.
- When she used to read fairy-tales, she fancied that kind of thing never happened, and now she is in the middle of one.
- She believes there ought to be a book written about her, and says that when she grows up she will write one; but she says she is grown up now and there is no room to grow up any more here.
- She fears she will never get any older than she is now, which is a comfort in one way (never to be an old woman) but she dislikes it because she would always have lessons to learn.
- She is now about a thousand times as large as the Rabbit and has no reason to be afraid of it.
- She trembled till she shook the house when she heard the Rabbit coming to look for her.
- Her elbow was pressed hard against the door, which kept it from opening inwards.
- She waited until she fancied she heard the Rabbit just under the window, then spread out her hand and made a snatch in the air.
- She did not get hold of anything, but heard a little shriek, a fall, and a crash of broken glass; she concluded it was just possible the thing had fallen into a cucumber-frame or something of the sort.
- She spread out her hand again and made another snatch in the air, which produced two little shrieks and more broken glass.
- She thinks there must be a great number of cucumber-frames, and wonders what they will do next.
- She does not want to stay in the room any longer.
- She waited for some time listening to the voices, then drew her foot as far down the chimney as she could.
- She believes "this fireplace is narrow", but thinks she can "kick a little".
- She thinks Bill "put everything upon Bill" and would not want to be in Bill's place for a good deal.
- She said to herself "This is Bill" and gave one sharp kick up the chimney, then waited to see what would happen next.
- She threatened to set Dinah at the others if they burn the house down.
- She thinks the others would take the roof off if they had any sense.
- She shouted at the attackers to stop throwing pebbles, and was hit in the face by some of them.
- She ate one of the pebble-cakes, believing it would make her smaller since it could not make her larger, and began shrinking directly.
- She ran out of the house once small enough to fit through the door, away from the crowd of little animals and birds, and escaped to a thick wood.
- She tried to coax the puppy with a whistle, and was terribly frightened that the puppy might be hungry and eat her.
- She picked up a little bit of stick and held it out to the puppy; she dodged behind a great thistle to avoid being run over, and eventually escaped from the puppy, running until she was quite tired and out of breath.
- She had been a dear little puppy's admirer and wished to teach it tricks.
- She is trying to figure out how to grow up again, and wonders what she ought to eat or drink to manage it.
- She leant against a buttercup to rest and fanned herself with one of its leaves.
- She stretched up on tiptoe to peep over the edge of the mushroom.
- She knows who she was when she got up that morning, but believes she has been changed several times since then.
- She had nearly forgotten that she has to grow up again.
- She finds being so many different sizes in a day very confusing, and cannot understand it herself.
- She thinks it would feel very queer to turn into a chrysalis and then a butterfly.
- She felt a little irritated at the Caterpillar's very short remarks.
- She asked the Caterpillar to tell her who it is first.
- She turned away from the Caterpillar, then came back when called; she swallowed down her anger as well as she could.
- She thought she might as well wait, as she had nothing else to do.
- She admits she is changed: she cannot remember things as she used, and does not keep the same size for ten minutes together.
- She tried to say "How doth the little busy bee" but it all came out different.
- She folded her hands and recited "You are old, Father William" when the Caterpillar asked her to repeat it.
- She is not particular as to size, but does not like changing so often; she has never been so much contradicted in her life before, and feels she is losing her temper.
- She would like to be a little larger; she finds three inches a wretched height, and says "But I'm not used to it!" in a piteous tone.
- She thinks "I wish the creatures wouldn't be so easily offended!"
- She waited patiently for the Caterpillar to speak again, wondering "One side of what? The other side of what?"
- She is shrinking rapidly and then grows a long neck; her head is free, which turns to alarm when she finds her shoulders gone.
- She tries to figure out which side of the mushroom is which, and nibbles bits of it to test the effects.
- She asks what the green stuff is, where her shoulders went, and where her poor hands are; she moves her hands, but nothing follows except a shaking among the distant green leaves.
- Her neck can bend easily in any direction, like a serpent; she is indignant at being called a serpent, and is puzzled by the Pigeon, though beginning to understand the Pigeon's meaning.
- She was wandering under trees and found the leaves to be the tops of those trees.
- She has tasted eggs, and says little girls eat eggs quite as much as serpents do.
- She is not looking for eggs and does not like raw eggs.
- Her neck keeps getting entangled among the branches of the trees, and she has to stop and untwist it.
- She holds pieces of mushroom in her hands, nibbles at them, and grows sometimes taller and sometimes shorter; she brings herself down to her usual height.
- She was quite silent for a minute or two after the Pigeon's remark about the new idea.
- She was not the right size for a long time, so it felt strange at first, but she got used to it in a few minutes.
- She says "Come, there's half my plan done now! How puzzling all these changes are! I'm never sure what I'm going to be, from one minute to another!"
- She has got back to her right size; her next goal is to get into the beautiful garden, and she wonders how that is to be done.
- She thinks it will never do to come upon the house occupants at her current size, because she would frighten them out of their wits.
- She nibbled the righthand bit again and brought herself down to nine inches high before going near the house.
- She was very curious to know what was going on with the footmen, and crept a little way out of the wood to listen.
- She considered the footman to be a footman because he was in livery; otherwise, judging by his face only, she would have called him a fish.
- She laughed greatly at the footmen's bowing and entangled curls, and ran back into the wood for fear of being heard.
- She peeped out, went timidly up to the door and knocked, and asked repeatedly how she is to get in.
- She thinks the Footman's upward gaze is decidedly uncivil, and wonders privately whether he cannot help it because his eyes are very nearly at the top of his head.
- She finds the way the creatures argue dreadful; it is enough to drive one crazy.
- She is not quite sure whether it is good manners to speak first, but takes courage and speaks.
- She sneezed from the pepper in the kitchen.
- She jumped when the Duchess spoke harshly to the baby.
- She did not know Cheshire cats always grinned, or that cats could grin.
- She felt quite pleased to have got into a conversation, but did not at all like the Duchess's tone of remark, and thought it would be as well to introduce some other subject.
- She was in an agony of terror and cried out "Oh, please mind what you're doing!"
- She knows that the earth takes twenty-four hours to turn round on its axis, but is unsure: "Twenty-four hours, I think; or is it twelve?"
- She does not know of any cats that can grin.
- She could hardly hear the words of the second verse because the baby howled.
- The baby is a queer-shaped little creature that holds out its arms and legs in all directions, "just like a star-fish"; for the first minute or two it is as much as she can do to hold it.
- She works out the proper way of nursing the baby: to twist it up into a sort of knot and keep tight hold of its right ear and left foot so it cannot undo itself.
- She carries the baby out into the open air and reasons that if she does not take it away with her, "they're sure to kill it in a day or two", and that leaving it behind would be murder.
- She scolds the baby for grunting, saying that is not a proper way of expressing oneself.

entities.name: Alice's sister
entities.description:
A tender, patient figure who sits beside a sleeping Alice on the riverbank, reading a book with no pictures or conversations in it.

Personality:
- Gentle and affectionate
- Patient and attentive; willing to sit and wait
- Listens to dreams with interest and warmth

Wants:
- Wake Alice gently and see her return to her tea

Knows:
- Alice has been asleep for a long time
- Alice's dream was curious
- The afternoon is getting late

Speech:
- Speaks softly and tenderly to Alice, using "dear"
- Gentle exclamations: "Wake up, Alice dear!" and "Why, what a long sleep you've had!"
- "It was a curious dream, dear, certainly: but now run in to your tea; it's getting late."

entities.name: White Rabbit
entities.description:
The White Rabbit: a rabbit with pink eyes, splendidly dressed, who carries a pair of white kid gloves in one hand and a large fan in the other, and who serves as herald at the trial with a trumpet in one hand and a scroll of parchment in the other. He is the first creature Alice sees at the start of her adventures, and he hurries through the long grass in the sister's dream. He has a waistcoat-pocket from which he takes a watch, looks at it, and hurries on.

Personality:
- Timid and anxious; peeps anxiously into Alice's face.
- Talks in a hurried, nervous manner, smiling at everything that is said.
- Respectful but frowning and making faces at the King.
- Starts violently when Alice speaks to him.
- Looks anxiously over his shoulder.
- Fears the Duchess will be savage if he has kept her waiting.
- Fears he will be executed by the Duchess.

Knows:
- Pops down a large rabbit-hole under the hedge.
- Hurries down a long passage and vanishes around a corner, out of Alice's view.
- Dropped the white kid gloves and the fan, and skurries away into the darkness when Alice speaks to him.
- Searches anxiously for the lost fan and pair of white kid gloves.
- Stands near the King at the court with a trumpet and a scroll of parchment.
- The Duchess is "under sentence of execution."
- The Duchess "boxed the Queen's ears."
- The Duchess came rather late, and the Queen said something.
- A paper has just been picked up at the trial; he believes it is a letter written by the prisoner to somebody, though he has not opened it yet.
- The paper was not directed at all, and there was nothing written on the outside.
- The paper is a set of verses, not a letter, and they are not in the prisoner's handwriting, which he calls "the queerest thing about it."
- The accusation reads: "The Queen of Hearts, she made some tarts, All on a summer day: The Knave of Hearts, he stole those tarts, And took them quite away!"
- Calls out "First witness!" and reads out the name "Alice!" as the next witness.
- Announces there is more evidence to come.

Speech:
- Mutters to himself in a hurry: "Oh dear! Oh dear! I shall be late!"
- "Oh my ears and whiskers, how late it's getting!"
- "Oh! the Duchess, the Duchess! Oh! won't she be savage if I've kept her waiting!"
- "The Duchess! The Duchess! Oh my dear paws! Oh my fur and whiskers! She'll get me executed, as sure as ferrets are ferrets! Where can I have dropped them, I wonder?"
- "It's—it's a very fine day!"
- Speaks in a low, hurried tone and rises on tiptoe to whisper in Alice's ear.
- Asks Alice if she said "What a pity!"
- Whispers in a frightened tone.
- Cries out "Silence in the court!"
- Hastily interrupts with "Not yet, not yet! There's a great deal to come before that!"
- Says in a low voice to the King: "Your Majesty must cross-examine this witness."
- Reads out at the top of his shrill little voice.
- Corrects "important" to "Unimportant, your Majesty means."
- Puts on his spectacles before reading.
- Asks "Where shall I begin, please your Majesty?"

entities.name: watch
entities.description:
Summary of the watches in the story:

- The White Rabbit takes a watch out of his waistcoat pocket, looks at it, and hurries on.
- The Hatter takes his watch from his pocket. He looks at it uneasily, shakes it now and then, and holds it to his ear.
- The March Hare uses a strange watch that shows the day of the month but not the hour. He dips it into his cup of tea.

entities.name: book
entities.description: Book read by Alice's sister; it has no pictures or conversations in it.

entities.name: daisies
entities.description: Flowers on the field that Alice considered picking to make a daisy-chain.

entities.name: bank
entities.description: Alice sits by her sister on a hot day, on a bank. The wet party gathers there. Birds have draggled feathers. Animals have fur clinging close. All are dripping wet, cross, and uncomfortable. They hold a consultation about how to get dry. Alice later lies with her head in her sister's lap after the pack of cards attacks.

entities.name: field
entities.description: Field across which Alice ran after the White Rabbit.

entities.name: rabbit-hole
entities.description: A large rabbit-hole lies under the hedge. It goes straight like a tunnel, then dips suddenly into a very deep well. Alice went down the hole and almost wishes she had not.

entities.name: hedge
entities.description:
This is from Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. Both descriptions refer to the same hedge.

The hedge is where the large rabbit-hole is located. One of the group is told to catch Bill near the hedge.

entities.name: deep well
entities.description: Very deep well into which Alice falls after the rabbit-hole dips suddenly down.

entities.name: The Well
entities.description: Alice falls slowly down a very deep, dark well. Its sides have cupboards, bookshelves, maps, and pictures hung on pegs. The Dormouse's three little sisters live at the bottom.

entities.name: cupboards
entities.description: Filled the sides of the well. Alice put the jar labelled 'ORANGE MARMALADE' into one of them as she fell past.

entities.name: book-shelves
entities.description: Filled the sides of the well. Alice took a jar labelled 'ORANGE MARMALADE' down from one of them as she passed.

entities.name: maps and pictures
entities.description: Hung upon pegs here and there on the sides of the well.

entities.name: ORANGE MARMALADE jar
entities.description: A jar labelled 'ORANGE MARMALADE', but to Alice's great disappointment it was empty. Alice placed it into one of the cupboards as she fell past.

entities.name: Schoolroom
entities.description: The place where Alice learnt several things of this sort in her lessons.

entities.name: Centre of the Earth
entities.description: The place Alice believes she must be getting somewhere near, estimating it to be about four thousand miles down.

entities.name: Dinah
entities.description:
Dinah: Alice's pet cat, a dear, quiet thing.

Personality:
- Dear and quiet; sits purring so nicely by the fire.
- Licks her paws and washes her face.
- A nice soft thing to nurse.
- A capital one for catching mice; will eat a little bird as soon as look at it.
- Alice considers her the best cat in the world.

Wants:
- Dinah is expected to miss Alice tonight.
- Alice wishes Dinah were down with her.

Knows:
- Alice hopes they will remember her saucer of milk at tea-time.
- There are no mice in the air, but Dinah might catch a bat, which is very like a mouse.
- Alice imagines asking Dinah whether she ever ate a bat.
- Alice supposes Dinah will be sending her on messages next.
- Alice doubts Dinah would be allowed to stay in the house if it began ordering people about like that.
- Alice threatens to set Dinah at the others.

Speech:
- Alice refers to her as "the best cat in the world."
- Alice notes that nobody seems to like her down here.

entities.name: Antipathies
entities.description: People who walk with their heads downward, on the other side of the earth, whom Alice thinks she might come out among. Alice would need to ask them the name of the country.

entities.name: Ma'am
entities.description: An unnamed person Alice addresses while falling, asking whether the country is New Zealand or Australia.

entities.name: New Zealand
entities.description: A country Alice asks about, wondering whether the place she is falling toward is this country.

entities.name: Australia
entities.description: A country Alice asks about, wondering whether the place she is falling toward is this country.

entities.name: bat
entities.description: A creature Alice thinks Dinah might catch in the air; Alice says it is very like a mouse. Alice repeatedly asks whether cats eat bats and whether bats eat cats.

entities.name: heap of sticks and dry leaves
entities.description: The place where Alice comes down with a thump, ending her fall.

entities.name: Long Passage
entities.description: Long passage before Alice after she jumped up; it was all dark overhead. The White Rabbit hurried down it.

entities.name: Long Hall
entities.description: A long, low hall is lit by a row of lamps hanging from the roof. Doors line all sides of the hall, and all of them are locked. Alice finds herself in this hall again, close to the little glass table.

entities.name: lamps
entities.description: A row of lamps hanging from the roof of the long, low hall, lighting it up.

entities.name: hall doors
entities.description: Doors all round the Long Hall; all were locked and none could be opened with the tiny golden key because the locks were too large or the key too small.

entities.name: three-legged table
entities.description: Little three-legged table, all made of solid glass. Had nothing on it except a tiny golden key.

entities.name: tiny golden key
entities.description: Tiny golden key lying on the solid glass three-legged table; would not open any of the hall doors. Fitted the lock of the little door behind the low curtain.

entities.name: low curtain
entities.description: Low curtain Alice had not noticed before on the second time round the hall; hides a little door about fifteen inches high.

entities.name: little door
entities.description:
Small door, about fifteen inches high, behind a low curtain. Its lock fits a tiny golden key.

Small door in a dark hall. It leads to a tiny passage, not much larger than a rat-hole. Alice cannot get her head through it.

Small door leads into a lovely garden. Alice is now the right size to go through, but it is locked. She has forgotten the tiny golden key.

Little door leads to the garden. It shuts again when Alice runs back to it.

Located in the great hall. It vanished completely.

entities.name: dark hall
entities.description: A dark hall containing a small door and a table. Alice is in it and longs to leave it.

entities.name: passage
entities.description: A small passage, not much larger than a rat-hole, leading from the little door. From it one can look along into the loveliest garden you ever saw.

entities.name: garden
entities.description: Alice sees a lovely garden with bright flowers and cool fountains. She longs to wander in it. She hopes to get in by reaching the key or creeping under the door. She looks into it through the little door with one eye. Alice finally reaches a beautiful garden. Five looks across the area where the gardeners work, watching for the Queen. A flamingo crosses to the other side, where Alice sees it trying to fly up into a tree.

entities.name: table
entities.description:
Tables in Wonderland:

1. A dark hall table holds a little bottle.
2. A table with slippery legs holds a golden key behind glass.
3. A table has a little glass box under it.
4. Alice measured herself against a table.
5. A tidy room's window table holds a fan and tiny white kid gloves.
6. A table is set for many guests, claimed by the March Hare to be his and the Hatter's.
7. A table in the court's center holds a large dish of tarts.

entities.name: little bottle
entities.description: A little bottle found on the table, which Alice believes was not there before. Round its neck is a paper label reading 'DRINK ME'. It is not known to be marked 'poison'; Alice intends to look first before drinking.

entities.name: DRINK ME label
entities.description: A paper label round the neck of the little bottle, with the words 'DRINK ME' beautifully printed on it in large letters.

entities.name: bottle
entities.description: Not marked 'poison'. Alice tasted it and found it very nice; it had a sort of mixed flavour of cherry-tart, custard, pine-apple, roast turkey, toffee, and hot buttered toast. Alice very soon finished it off.

entities.name: lovely garden
entities.description: A lovely garden lies behind a little door. Alice intends to enter it after she grows to the right size.

entities.name: little golden key
entities.description: A little golden key sits on the glass table, visible but out of Alice's reach. Alice forgets it at the door. Later, she takes the key and uses it to unlock the garden door.

entities.name: glass
entities.description: Transparent; the little golden key could be seen plainly through it.

entities.name: little glass box
entities.description: A little glass box lying under the table. Alice opened it and found a very small cake inside.

entities.name: cake
entities.description:
Cake from a little glass box, with "EAT ME" spelled in currants. Alice ate it all. It did not change her size.

Small cakes that pebbles turn into on the floor. Eating one makes Alice shrink.

entities.name: key
entities.description: A key that Alice hopes to reach if the cake makes her grow larger.

entities.name: door
entities.description:
Doors in Alice's adventure:

- A small door Alice can creep under if she shrinks.
- Once Alice grows large, she cannot get out this way. She lies down with her elbow pressed against it.
- A door that opens inward. The Rabbit tries to open it but fails because Alice's elbow blocks it.
- The house door. Alice must be small enough to fit through it.
- The house door, near which a footman sits. Alice knocks here. A large plate later flies out of it.
- Alice opens this door and goes in. It leads straight into the kitchen.

entities.name: Alice's feet
entities.description: Alice's feet, which seem almost out of sight from her point of view because she is so far off. Alice refers to them as 'my poor little feet' and 'dears'. She wonders who will put on their shoes and stockings, and she thinks they may not walk the way she wants to go unless she is kind to them.

entities.name: the hall
entities.description: A hall has a roof and a garden door. A large pool reaches halfway down its length. The pool is about four inches deep. It is very hot.

entities.name: garden door
entities.description: A door in the long hall leads to the garden. Alice unlocks it with a little golden key. Getting through it is hopeless for Alice.

entities.name: large pool of tears
entities.description: A large pool, about four inches deep, reaching half down the hall, formed from Alice's shedding gallons of tears.

entities.name: Christmas
entities.description: The occasion on which Alice plans to give her feet a new pair of boots every year.

entities.name: Alice's Right Foot, Esq., Hearthrug, near the Fender
entities.description: A hypothetical address Alice imagines writing on a parcel of presents sent by the carrier to her right foot, with the note '(with Alice's love)'.

entities.name: Duchess
entities.description:
The Duchess: a very ugly woman with an uncomfortably sharp chin, the exact height to rest it on Alice's shoulder. She sits on a three-legged stool in the middle of the kitchen, nursing a baby that sneezes on her knee while plates and dishes crash around it, and she sneezes occasionally from the pepper. Objects thrown at her don't bother her, even when they hit. She was in prison and was fetched by the executioner at the Queen's order. The White Rabbit fears she will be savage if he has kept her waiting, or that she will get him executed. She boxed the Queen's ears, came rather late, and was in a pleasant temper when she walked off arm in arm with Alice.

Personality:
- Speaks harshly and in a hoarse growl.
- Savage in the kitchen, but in a pleasant temper later; she is fond of finding morals in everything.
- Believes everything has a moral, if only you can find it.
- Believes that if everybody minded their own business, the world would go round a deal faster than it does.
- Thinks Alice has as much right to think as pigs have to fly.
- Is doubtful about the temper of Alice's flamingo.
- Seems ready to agree to everything Alice says.
- Speaks of forgetting to talk when someone is thinking.

Wants:
- To get ready to play croquet with the Queen.
- To have her child nursed, and to pass the baby to Alice ("Here! you may nurse it a bit, if you like!").

Knows:
- She is the recipient of the great letter, an invitation from the Queen to play croquet.
- She is under sentence of execution, according to the White Rabbit.
- Cats always grin, "and most of 'em do."
- The Cheshire cat grins "and that's why."
- Flamingoes and mustard both bite.
- There is a large mustard-mine near here.
- Her child is a pig-baby.
- She makes a "present" of everything she has said so far, which Alice privately thinks is a cheap present.

Secret:
- None stated.

Speech:
- "Pig!" (said to the baby)
- "Talking of axes, chop off her head!"
- "They all can, and most of 'em do."
- "You don't know much, and that's a fact."
- "If everybody minded their own business, the world would go round a deal faster than it does."
- "Oh, don't bother me," and "I never could abide figures!"
- Lullaby sung with a violent shake at the end of every line; tosses the baby violently up and down during the second verse.
- "Here! you may nurse it a bit, if you like!"
- "I must go and get ready to play croquet with the Queen."
- "You can't think how glad I am to see you again, you dear old thing!"
- "Tut, tut, child!"
- "Oh, 'tis love, 'tis love, that makes the world go round!"
- "Take care of the sense, and the sounds will take care of themselves."
- "Birds of a feather flock together."
- "The more there is of mine, the less there is of yours."
- "Be what you would seem to be."
- "Ah, well! It means much the same thing."
- "Right, as usual," and "what a clear way you have of putting things!"
- Says she could say more if she chose, in a pleased tone.
- Greets the Queen with "A fine day, your Majesty!" in a low, weak voice.

entities.name: white kid gloves
entities.description: The White Rabbit dropped a pair of white kid gloves. Alice picked them up. Two or three pairs lie on the table in the tidy little room. Alice takes one pair.

entities.name: fan
entities.description:
A large fan was dropped by the White Rabbit. Alice picked it up and used it to fan herself. Later, Alice held the fan and it made her shrink. She dropped it quickly to avoid shrinking away completely.

The White Rabbit was looking for a lost item. Alice guessed it was being sought, but it could not be found. The Rabbit asked Alice to fetch it, and she planned to take it to him if she could find it. It lay on the table in the tidy little room, where Alice picked it up.

entities.name: darkness
entities.description: The place into which the White Rabbit skurried away as hard as he could go.

entities.name: Ada
entities.description: Mentioned by Alice as someone whose hair goes in such long ringlets. Alice is sure she is not Ada.

entities.name: Mabel
entities.description: Mentioned by Alice as someone who knows such a very little. Alice believes she must be Mabel after all, and that Mabel would live in a poky little house with next to no toys and many lessons to learn.

entities.name: How doth the little crocodile
entities.description: A poem Alice tries to repeat. Verses: 'How doth the little crocodile / Improve his shining tail, / And pour the waters of the Nile / On every golden scale!' and 'How cheerfully he seems to grin, / How neatly spread his claws, / And welcome little fishes in / With gently smiling jaws!' Alice says these are not the right words.

entities.name: Multiplication Table
entities.description: A body of knowledge Alice tries to recall; she says it 'doesn't signify' and turns to Geography instead.

entities.name: poky little house
entities.description: A house Alice believes she would have to go and live in if she is Mabel. Described as poky and little; she would have next to no toys to play with there.

entities.name: down here
entities.description: The place where Alice says she will stay if she is Mabel, and where she says she is all alone and very tired of being alone.

entities.name: Rabbit's little white kid gloves
entities.description: A pair of little white kid gloves belonging to the Rabbit; one of them was put on by Alice without her realizing it while she was talking.

entities.name: glass table
entities.description: A glass table holds a little golden key. It was in the great hall and has vanished completely.

entities.name: sea
entities.description:
The sea is where Alice thought she fell. Seaside places on the English coast have bathing machines, children digging in sand with wooden spades, lodging houses, and a railway station.

Lobster Quadrille dancers throw lobsters as far out as they can. They swim after them and turn a somersault.

Lobsters and turtles are thrown into the sea when the dancers take them up.

Whiting were thrown out into the sea. Crumbs washed off there.

The location of the Mock Turtle's school is not stated.

entities.name: railway
entities.description: A railway by which Alice said she could go back if she had fallen into the sea.

entities.name: pool of tears
entities.description: A pool of salt water made of the tears Alice had wept when she was nine feet high, in which she found herself up to her chin.

entities.name: Mouse
entities.description:
The Mouse: a mouse that slipped into the pool with Alice, later the speaker of a long history lesson in Alice in Wonderland. Pale-faced, bristling, with a tail that trembles.

Personality:
- Severe and easily offended; bristles all over when offended and trembles down to the end of its tail.
- Speaks with an important air and expects silence all round.
- Frowns but speaks very politely when interrupted.
- Looks at Alice rather inquisitively and seems to wink with one of its little eyes, but initially says nothing.
- Shrill, passionate voice; becomes cross quickly.
- Gets up and walks away, growls in reply, shakes its head impatiently, and walks a little quicker when offended.
- Dislikes cats and dogs; its family always hated cats.
- A frightened creature that splashes about in the pool; gives a sudden leap out of the water and quivers all over with fright when Alice says 'Où est ma chatte?'.
- Seemed to be a person of authority among the birds and animals.
- Appears to be a French mouse to Alice's guess (not confirmed), and does not seem to understand English per Alice's thought.
- Has a tail (Alice wonders at it).

Wants:
- Silence all round so it can read a history passage it calls 'the driest thing I know'.
- Alice's prize must be given to her, as she must have one herself; the Mouse says "But she must have a prize herself, you know."
- Not to hear the name of cats again.
- To tell Alice its history, so she will understand why it hates cats and dogs.

Knows:
- - Reads aloud from a history text about William the Conqueror, Edwin and Morcar, Stigand, Edgar Atheling and the Normans.
- Its tale is told through a poem about Fury and a mouse, in which Fury, cunning old Fury, a cur, prosecutes the mouse, acts as judge and jury, and condemns the mouse to death.
- Mistakes 'bend' for 'a knot' in a sense; refuses Alice's offer to help undo it, saying 'I shall do nothing of the sort'.
- Has a long and a sad tale to tell.
- Does not answer the Duck's question about what the archbishop found; becomes cross when asked, saying 'of course you know what it means'.
- Does not answer Alice's question about dogs.

Secret:
- Its family always hated cats, calling them nasty, low, vulgar things; the reason it hates cats and dogs is in its history, which it has not finished telling.

Speech:
- Shrill, passionate voice when excited; low trembling voice when telling its history.
- Asks Alice: 'Would you like cats if you were me?'
- Says 'I had not!' sharply and angrily when Alice says he had got to the fifth bend.
- Says 'I shall do nothing of the sort' and that Alice insults it with nonsense.
- Calls Alice 'my dear' and asks how she is getting on.
- Called out "Sit down, all of you, and listen to me! I'll soon make you dry enough!"
- Spoke: "Let us get to the shore, and then I'll tell you my history, and you'll understand why it is I hate cats and dogs."
- Says 'of course you know what it means' when asked about the archbishop.
- Mentioned in Alice's imagined dialogue: Alice says she has to see that the mouse doesn't get out.
- A frightened creature that splashes his way through the neighbouring pool in the sister's dream.

entities.name: The Pool
entities.description: The pool is where Alice and the Mouse swim. Alice swims nearer to the Mouse, a little way from her position, and wants to find the way out. Alice swims lazily here while the Mouse swims away, making a commotion. The pool becomes crowded with birds and animals that fell in. Alice, the Mouse, and the others swim from it to the shore. Alice later returns to the place of her swim and finds everything changed. A neighbouring pool is where the frightened Mouse splashes, though it only ripples from the waving reeds.

entities.name: Latin Grammar
entities.description: Alice's brother's Latin Grammar. Contains the example 'A mouse—of a mouse—to a mouse—a mouse—O mouse!'.

entities.name: French lesson-book
entities.description: Alice's French lesson-book. Its first sentence is 'Où est ma chatte?'.

entities.name: Où est ma chatte?
entities.description: French sentence meaning 'Where is my cat?', the first sentence in Alice's French lesson-book. Spoken by Alice to the Mouse, causing it to leap out of the water in fright.

entities.name: William the Conqueror
entities.description:
A figure mentioned by Alice, whose arrival in England may have brought a French mouse over. No other details given.

Personality:
- His conduct at first was moderate, but the insolence of his Normans is mentioned.

Knows:
- His arrival in England may have brought a French mouse over (as mentioned by Alice).
- His cause was favoured by the pope.
- The English were soon submitted to him.
- He went to meet with Edgar Atheling and was offered the crown.

entities.name: Cats
entities.description:
Cheshire Cat: a talking cat that appears and vanishes suddenly, leaving its grin behind. It sits on a branch of a tree and speaks to Alice. Its head began fading away the moment the executioner left, and by the time the executioner returned with the Duchess it had entirely disappeared.

Knows:
- The Mouse dislikes cats and dogs, which it describes as nasty, low, vulgar things. The Mouse's family always hated them.
- Alice's cat Dinah is one of the animals the Mouse dislikes.
- The Cat vanishes slowly, beginning with the end of the tail and ending with the grin, which remains some time after the rest of it has gone.
- The Cat's head is the thing the King and executioner searched for.
- The Cat is the subject of the dispute over whether it belongs to the Duchess.

Speech:
- "You must be, or you wouldn't have come here."
- Argues that a dog is not mad, because a dog growls when angry and wags its tail when pleased.
- "I growl when I'm pleased, and wag my tail when I'm angry. Therefore I'm mad."
- "Call it what you like." (said when Alice says purring, not growling)
- "Do you play croquet with the Queen to-day?"
- "You'll see me there."
- "By-the-bye, what became of the baby?"
- "I thought it would." (when told the baby turned into a pig)
- "Did you say pig, or fig?"
- "All right."

entities.name: fire
entities.description: A fire by which Dinah sits purring.

entities.name: Alice's house
entities.description: Alice's home. A nice little dog lives near it.

entities.name: terrier
entities.description: A nice little dog near Alice's house. A little bright-eyed terrier with oh, such long curly brown hair. Will fetch things when thrown, will sit up and beg for its dinner, and does all sorts of things. Belongs to a farmer. The farmer says it is so useful and worth a hundred pounds. The farmer says it kills all the rats.

entities.name: farmer
entities.description: Owns the terrier. Says the terrier is so useful and worth a hundred pounds, and that it kills all the rats.

entities.name: Duck
entities.description:
This is the Dodo from Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, as described in these two passages.

Personality:
- Not stated in the text.

Wants:
- Not stated in the text.

Knows:
- It fell into the pool with the other birds and animals.
- It was among the party that swam to the shore.
- When it finds a thing, it is "generally a frog or a worm."

Speech:
- Asks what the archbishop found.
- Its question is not answered by the Mouse.

entities.name: Dodo
entities.description:
Persona sheet: The Dodo, a bird from the pool of animals in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, who presides over the Caucus-race.

Personality:
- Solemn and grave in manner, rising to its feet with dignity to make motions.
- Offended in tone when speaking.
- Dignified and formal, given to long pauses for thought.

Wants:
- To get the wet party dry by the fastest and most energetic means available.
- To present prizes to everyone who has taken part in the race.

Knows:
- A bird that had fallen into the pool with the other birds and animals.
- Among the party that swam to the shore.
- The best thing to get the group dry would be a Caucus-race.
- A Caucus-race is run by marking out a race-course in a sort of circle ("the exact shape doesn't matter") and placing all the party along the course, here and there.
- In a Caucus-race there is no "One, two, three, and away"; participants begin running when they like and leave off when they like.
- The race ends after about half an hour, when everyone is quite dry again.
- Everybody has won, and all must have prizes.

Secret:
- Cannot answer "But who has won?" without a great deal of thought; sits a long time with one finger pressed upon its forehead (the position in which you usually see Shakespeare in pictures).

Speech:
- Offended in tone when speaking; grave and very solemn.
- Explains things by doing them, calling out "The race is over!" when the race ends.
- Pointedly addresses others with one finger raised, as when pointing to Alice ("she").
- Formal, ceremonious phrasing, such as "We beg your acceptance of this elegant thimble."
- Asks Alice what else she has in her pocket and asks her to hand over the thimble.
- Organizes the group to crowd around Alice and cheer after a speech.

entities.name: Lory
entities.description:
A bird from the pool of tears, with draggled feathers, who has appeared in several scenes.

Personality:
- Sulky and touchy when challenged; takes offense easily.
- Haughty about its seniority, insisting on its superior knowledge.
- Shy and easily flustered when others notice it.
- Polite and deferential when asking questions.

Wants:
- To be treated as wiser and more experienced than Alice.
- To ask who Dinah is, politely, if it may venture the question.

Knows:
- Who Dinah is.
- Its own age, though it refuses to tell it.

Secret:
- It was the one who said "Ugh!" with a shiver when the Mouse began reading, and it denies having spoken when the Mouse asks whether it did.

Speech:
- "I am older than you, and must know better."
- "Ugh!" (said with a shiver)
- "What a pity it wouldn't stay!" (sighed once the Mouse is out of sight)
- Politely asks, "May I venture to ask who Dinah is?"

entities.name: Eaglet
entities.description:
A young eagle who fell into the pool with the other birds and animals and was among the party that swam to the shore.

Personality:
- Blunt and impatient with pretension; it does not hide its scorn for big words.
- Hides its amusement by bending its head down to conceal a smile.

Knows:
- It fell into the pool with the other birds and animals.
- It swam to the shore with the party.

Speech:
- Tells the Dodo "Speak English!"
- Says it doesn't know the meaning of half the long words the Dodo uses.
- Doubts the Dodo knows the meaning of those long words either.

entities.name: shore
entities.description: Destination the party swam to from the pool. The Mouse promised to tell its history once they reached the shore.

entities.name: Caucus-Race and a Long Tale
entities.description: Title of Chapter III. Chapter in which the wet party assembles on the bank and discusses how to get dry.

entities.name: other birds
entities.description: Some of the other birds tittered audibly at the Eaglet's remark.

entities.name: Edwin
entities.description: Earl of Mercia (named with Morcar as 'the earls of Mercia and Northumbria'). Declared for William.

entities.name: Morcar
entities.description: Earl of Northumbria (named with Edwin as 'the earls of Mercia and Northumbria'). Declared for William.

entities.name: Stigand
entities.description: The patriotic archbishop of Canterbury. Found it advisable to go with Edgar Atheling to meet William and offer him the crown.

entities.name: Edgar Atheling
entities.description: Went with Stigand to meet William and offer him the crown.

entities.name: Normans
entities.description: The people of William the Conqueror, whose insolence is mentioned in the history passage.

entities.name: English
entities.description: Submitted to William the Conqueror; wanted leaders and had been much accustomed to usurpation and conquest.

entities.name: history passage
entities.description: A dry text read aloud by the Mouse about William the Conqueror, Edwin and Morcar, Stigand, Edgar Atheling and the Normans. Begins with 'William the Conqueror, whose cause was favoured by the pope, was soon submitted to by the English'.

entities.name: Caucus-race
entities.description: The Dodo proposed a race to get the party dry. The race ran along a circular course with no start signal. Participants ran when and as long as they liked. It was hard to know when it ended.

entities.name: race-course
entities.description: Marked out by the Dodo in a sort of circle; the exact shape doesn't matter. All the party were placed along it, here and there.

entities.name: box of comfits
entities.description: Pulled out of Alice's pocket; salt water had not got into it. Handed round as prizes, exactly one a-piece.

entities.name: thimble
entities.description: Alice's only possession in her pocket. Described by the Dodo as an elegant thimble. Presented to Alice by the Dodo as a prize and taken by Alice.

entities.name: comfits
entities.description: Sweets that the group eats together, causing noise and confusion. The large birds could not taste theirs, and the small ones choked and had to be patted on the back.

entities.name: large birds
entities.description: Part of the group gathered in the ring. Complained that they could not taste their comfits.

entities.name: small birds
entities.description: Part of the group gathered in the ring. Choked on their comfits and had to be patted on the back.

entities.name: Fury
entities.description: A cur, described as cunning old Fury. In the Mouse's poem, says to a mouse that they should both go to law and that Fury will prosecute the mouse. Insists on a trial, saying nothing else is to be done that morning. Declares that Fury will be judge and jury, will try the whole cause, and will condemn the mouse to death.

entities.name: Mouse's history
entities.description: The long and sad tale the Mouse promised to tell Alice. Presented as a poem about Fury and a mouse who meet in the house, in which Fury prosecutes the mouse and condemns it to death in a trial with no jury or judge.

entities.name: eating the comfits
entities.description: The next activity after the thimble presentation. Caused some noise and confusion; afterward the group sat down again in a ring and begged the Mouse to tell them something more.

entities.name: old Crab
entities.description: Mother of the young Crab. Takes the opportunity to tell her daughter: 'Ah, my dear! Let this be a lesson to you never to lose your temper!'

entities.name: young Crab
entities.description: Daughter of the old Crab. Replies a little snappishly: 'Hold your tongue, Ma!' and says her mother is 'enough to try the patience of an oyster!'

entities.name: Party of birds
entities.description: A group of birds that caused a sensation among the party after the speech; some hurried off at once, and all moved off on various pretexts, leaving Alice alone.

entities.name: Magpie
entities.description: An old Magpie who began wrapping itself up very carefully, remarking, 'I really must be getting home; the night-air doesn't suit my throat!'

entities.name: Canary
entities.description: A Canary that called out in a trembling voice to its children, 'Come away, my dears! It's high time you were all in bed!'

entities.name: pair of white kid gloves
entities.description: Lost item the White Rabbit was looking for; could not be found.

entities.name: great hall
entities.description: A great hall with a glass table and a little door that had vanished completely.

entities.name: Rabbit
entities.description:
The White Rabbit, a fussy, hurried rabbit who orders others about and is also heard as a gruff voice from the house and a figure trapped in the window.

Personality:
- Hurried and fussy, ordering others about
- Angry and scolding
- Cowardly toward Pat
- Gruff in tone

Wants:
- Gloves and a fan fetched at once
- Help getting out of the house ("this!")
- Pat to take the arm away from the window
- Alice to be removed, and the house burned down, to deal with the intruder

Knows:
- Owns a neat little house with a bright brass plate engraved 'W. RABBIT' on the door
- Believed Alice was his housemaid, Mary Ann
- Alice thinks he will be surprised when he finds out who she is
- Is about a thousand times smaller than Alice
- The door opens inwards, and Alice's elbow was pressed against it
- Plans to go round and get in at the window, saying to himself 'Then I'll go round and get in at the window.'
- Calls out 'Pat! Pat! Where are you?' from just under the window
- Scolds Pat for 'Digging for apples'
- Calls the arm 'an arm, you goose!'
- Remarks that the arm fills the whole window and has no business there
- Calls Pat a coward
- Gives orders during the rescue of Bill
- Is part of the group of voices talking together
- Says 'We must burn the house down!'
- Says 'A barrowful will do, to begin with.'
- Is part of a group that moves about and throws pebbles through the window
- Is referred to as 'the Rabbit' in the text
- Voice heard calling 'Catch him, you by the hedge!' after Alice's kick

Secret:
- Stuck or trapped in the house, needing help getting out

Speech:
- Angry, hurried, and scolding
- Says 'Pat! Pat! Where are you?'
- Says 'Then I'll go round and get in at the window.'
- Says 'an arm, you goose!'
- Says 'this!' when asking for help

entities.name: Mary Ann
entities.description:
Mary Ann, the real maid of the house, whom the Rabbit mistakenly calls Alice.

Wants:
- The Rabbit orders her to fetch its gloves "this moment."

Knows:
- Alice fears meeting her in the house.

entities.name: neat little house
entities.description: A neat little house with a bright brass plate on its door engraved with the name 'W. RABBIT'. Alice went in without knocking and hurried upstairs.

entities.name: bright brass plate
entities.description: Bright brass plate on the door of the neat little house, engraved with the name 'W. RABBIT'.

entities.name: pair of gloves
entities.description: Requested by the Rabbit to be fetched by Alice; Alice intends to take them to him, if she can find them.

entities.name: Tidy Little Room
entities.description: A tidy little room with a table in the window. On the table (as Alice had hoped) lie a fan and two or three pairs of tiny white kid gloves. A little bottle stands near the looking-glass. Alice leaves the room after taking the fan and a pair of gloves, but the room is so small that she cannot get out of it once she has grown large.

entities.name: looking-glass
entities.description: Stands in the tidy little room. The little bottle stands near it.

entities.name: little magic bottle
entities.description: A little bottle with no label this time (no 'DRINK ME' label). Stands near the looking-glass. Alice uncorks it and drinks from it. It makes her grow large, much sooner than she expected, and its full effect stops her growing. Alice hastily put it down after drinking, having drunk about half of it. It is magic.

entities.name: ceiling
entities.description: Alice's head presses against it after she grows from drinking the little magic bottle.

entities.name: window
entities.description: The table stands in the tidy little room's window. Alice puts one arm out of the window as a last resort. The Rabbit says it will go round and get in through the window. Alice is stuck in the window, and the Rabbit is just under it. Her arm fills the whole window. Glass in the window breaks during the events. A shower of little pebbles rattles in through the window of the house.

entities.name: chimney
entities.description: Alice, growing large, puts one foot up the chimney as a last resort. The chimney is a narrow one above a fireplace. A little animal, Bill, is scrambling in it close above Alice.

entities.name: house
entities.description:
Alice is in a house. The Rabbit comes to its door. Alice trembles until the house shakes.

The Rabbit's group threatens to burn the house down. The house has a door and a window. Alice runs out through the door once she is small enough to fit.

The house has a door that opens to release a large plate. Inside, there is constant howling and sneezing. Every now and then, a great crash sounds, as if a dish or kettle broke.

entities.name: stairs
entities.description: Stairs in the house on which there was a little pattering of feet as the Rabbit came up.

entities.name: gloves
entities.description: The Rabbit's gloves, which it ordered Mary Ann to fetch.

entities.name: fairy-tales
entities.description: Stories Alice used to read, in which she fancied that kind of thing never happened.

entities.name: lesson-books
entities.description: Books for lessons, of which there is no room for any in the house, according to Alice.

entities.name: Pat
entities.description: Servant-like character with an Irish-style speech, who answers 'Sure then I'm here! Digging for apples, yer honour!' He pronounces 'arm' as 'arrum'. He identifies the object in the window as 'an arm, yer honour!' and says 'it's an arm for all that'. He says 'I don't like it, yer honour, at all, at all!' and is ordered by the Rabbit to take the arm away. He is reluctant and fearful.

entities.name: arm
entities.description: Arm that fills the whole window. Pat says it is 'an arm for all that'. The Rabbit says it has no business there and orders it taken away. Alice snatches at it in the air.

entities.name: cucumber-frame
entities.description: Structure into which Alice concludes the falling object may have fallen, causing a crash of broken glass. Alice believes there must be many of them.

entities.name: Bill
entities.description:
Bill the Lizard, a little animal whose exact kind Alice cannot guess, later described as "the unfortunate little Bill."

Personality:
- Feeble and flustered, speaks in a weak, squeaking voice.
- Dutifully carries on his task even when it is painful or absurd, hastily resuming writing with whatever is at hand.

Wants:
- Nothing stated beyond following orders from the others.

Knows:
- Is scratching and scrambling about in the chimney close above Alice.
- Was sent down the chimney by the others ("the master says you're to go down the chimney").
- Had left off writing on his slate with one finger because it made no mark.
- Hastily began writing again using the ink trickling down his face, for as long as it lasted.
- Was kicked by Alice, then fell out with a general chorus of "There goes Bill!"

Secret:
- None stated.

Speech:
- Speaks in a little feeble, squeaking voice.
- "Well, I hardly know—No more, thank ye; I'm better now—but I'm a deal too flustered to tell you—all I know is, something comes at me like a Jack-in-the-box, and up I goes like a sky-rocket!"
- Others address him with "Hold up his head," "Don't choke him," and "What happened to you? Tell us all about it!"

entities.name: roof
entities.description: The roof that the group are working on; they ask 'Will the roof bear?' and warn 'Mind that loose slate'.

entities.name: loose slate
entities.description: A loose slate on the roof. Warned about by the group ('Mind that loose slate'). Comes down, causing a loud crash ('Oh, it's coming down! Heads below!').

entities.name: ladders
entities.description: Ladders being brought and put up at a corner, and tied together. Described as not reaching half high enough yet, but said to 'do well enough'. One ladder was brought, and Bill has the other.

entities.name: rope
entities.description: A rope that Bill is told to catch hold of.

entities.name: brandy
entities.description: Given to Bill to help him recover after his fall ('Brandy now').

entities.name: Bill the Lizard
entities.description:
Bill the Lizard, a poor little lizard held up in the middle of a crowd of small animals and birds by two guinea-pigs, who are giving it something out of a bottle.
One of the jurors, a character at the trial.

Personality:
- Not described.

Wants:
- Not described.

Knows:
- Did not know how to spell 'stupid' and had to ask his neighbour.

Secret:
- Not described.

Speech:
- Not described.

entities.name: guinea-pigs
entities.description:
Two guinea-pigs from the court of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, who cheer and are then suppressed by the court officers.

Personality:
- Eager and rowdy; they cheer at the wrong moments and are immediately suppressed by the officers of the court.

Knows:
- Not stated.

Secret:
- Not stated.

Speech:
- Not stated; they cheer rather than speak.

Wants:
- Not stated.

Appearance and scene details:
- Two guinea-pigs holding up Bill the Lizard and giving it something out of a bottle.
- They make a rush at Alice when she appears.
- One guinea-pig cheered and was immediately suppressed by the officers of the court.
- Put into a large canvas bag head first and sat upon by officers.
- A second guinea-pig also cheered and was suppressed.
- One of the guinea-pigs is in the court while the other cheers and is suppressed.
- Suppressed guinea-pigs whose choking fills the air in the sister's dream.

entities.name: little animals and birds
entities.description: A crowd waiting outside the house; they make a rush at Alice the moment she appears.

entities.name: pebbles
entities.description: Little pebbles thrown in at the window, rattling in and hitting Alice in the face; they turn into little cakes as they lie on the floor.

entities.name: the thick wood
entities.description: A thick wood where Alice runs off and finds herself safe; she wanders about in it.

entities.name: puppy
entities.description:
A large puppy with big round eyes, and a sharp but feeble bark.

Personality:
- Playful and eager, leaping and yelping with delight at a stick.
- Makes believe to worry the stick, tumbles head over heels in its hurry to grab it, and makes short hoarse-barking charges at it.
- Tires quickly: finally sits down at a distance, panting, tongue hanging out, great eyes half shut.
- Affectionate and friendly toward Alice, stretching out one paw trying to touch her.

Wants:
- To play with the stick and get hold of it.
- To touch Alice with its paw.

Knows:
- Nothing specified.

Speech:
- Barks sharply but feebly; its bark fades into the distance as Alice runs away.

entities.name: stick
entities.description: A little bit of stick that Alice picks up and holds out to the puppy as a lure.

entities.name: great thistle
entities.description: A great thistle behind which Alice dodges to keep herself from being run over by the puppy; she runs round it again later.

entities.name: trees
entities.description:
Alice peers anxiously among the trees. The puppy is above her head.

Alice crouches among the trees. Her neck gets tangled in the branches.

A flamingo tries helplessly to fly into a tree.

entities.name: buttercup
entities.description: A buttercup Alice leaned against to rest herself; she fanned herself with one of its leaves.

entities.name: large mushroom
entities.description: Growing near Alice, about the same height as her. Alice looked under it, on both sides of it, and behind it, and then on its top, where a large blue caterpillar was sitting.

entities.name: Caterpillar
entities.description:
Large blue caterpillar sitting on a large mushroom, with folded arms and a long hookah, which it smokes and sometimes takes out of its mouth.
Personality: Languid, sleepy, stern, contemptuous and in a very unpleasant state of mind; decided and contradicts Alice; yawns, shakes itself and turns away without ceremony.
Wants: To know who Alice is and to have Alice explain herself; to ask Alice what size she wants to be; to know whether Alice is content now; to hear Alice recite "You are old, Father William" and to judge it.
Knows:
- One side of the mushroom will make you grow taller, and the other side will make you grow shorter.
- Alice will feel a little queer when turning into a chrysalis and then a butterfly (it says it will not feel queer at all).
- Being many sizes in a day is not confusing.
- Its own height is exactly three inches, which it says is a very good height indeed.
- The "You are old, Father William" recitation came out wrong; "That is not said right," and "It is wrong from beginning to end."
- It asks Alice what things she can't remember.
Secret: Which side of the mushroom makes you taller and which makes you shorter; it answers only "Of the mushroom" when asked which side is which.
Speech: Very short remarks; languid, sleepy voice; stern and curt. Phrases include "Who are you?", "I don't see", "Keep your temper", "I don't know", "You'll get used to it in time", "Are you content now?", and "Of the mushroom." Asks Alice to explain herself and asks whether she thinks she is changed. Says Alice should not be asked why and that it has something important to say. Puffs away without speaking for some minutes before speaking again. Unfolds its arms when addressing Alice. Yawns, shakes itself, gets down off the mushroom, crawls away in the grass, and disappears out of sight.

entities.name: hookah
entities.description: A long hookah is smoked by the Caterpillar. The Caterpillar takes it out of its mouth to speak to Alice. It puts the hookah into its mouth and takes it out again.

entities.name: Father William
entities.description:
Father William, an old man with very white hair and grey locks, who is fat and old. He is the subject of the poem "You Are Old, Father William," which Alice repeated to the Caterpillar.

Personality:
- A sage.
- In his youth he feared that standing on his head might injure his brain, but now he is perfectly sure he has none, so he does it again and again.
- Old and fat, yet he turned a back-somersault in at the door.

Knows:
- Incessantly stands on his head.
- Keeps his limbs supple with an ointment sold at one shilling the box and offers to sell a couple.
- Has very weak jaws, yet finished a goose with the bones and beak.
- In his youth he took to the law and argued each case with his wife; the muscular strength this gave his jaw has lasted the rest of his life.
- Balanced an eel on the end of his nose.
- Has answered three questions and refuses more.

Speech:
- Tells his son "don't give yourself airs!"
- Threatens "Be off, or I'll kick you down stairs!"

entities.name: youth
entities.description: Son of Father William. Questions his father: says he is old, with white hair, and stands on his head; that he has grown most uncommonly fat; that his jaws are too weak for anything tougher than suet; that his eye is as steady as ever; asks why he turned a back-somersault, how he finished the goose, and what made him so awfully clever.

entities.name: ointment
entities.description: Sold by Father William at one shilling the box. Keeps limbs very supple when used.

entities.name: You Are Old, Father William
entities.description: Poem recited by Alice at the Caterpillar's request, in which the youth questions Father William and Father William answers.

entities.name: mushroom
entities.description:
The Caterpillar sits on a round object and gets down off it before crawling away. Its hint says one side makes you grow taller and the other makes you grow shorter.

The object is perfectly round, with two sides and an edge. Alice breaks off a bit of the edge with each hand. Eating the right-hand bit strikes her foot violently under her chin. Eating the left-hand bit makes her grow. At one point, she shrinks rapidly.

Alice nibbles it until she is about a foot high. She had kept a piece in her pocket.

entities.name: grass
entities.description: The caterpillar crawls away in the grass and goes out of sight. The long grass rustles at the sister's feet. It rustles only in the wind.

entities.name: right-hand bit
entities.description: Alice nibbles a bit of the mushroom, broken off by her right hand, to change her size. Nibbling it makes her foot strike her chin violently. She uses it to bring herself down to nine inches high.

entities.name: lefthand bit
entities.description: A bit of the mushroom's edge broken off by Alice's left hand. Swallowing a morsel of it frees her head.

entities.name: green leaves
entities.description: A sea of green leaves far below Alice, from which an immense length of neck rises like a stalk; distant leaves shake when Alice moves her hands.

entities.name: Pigeon
entities.description:
A large, violent pigeon who lives in a nest atop the highest tree in the wood and has a long, serpent-shaped neck of its own in mind when it judges others.

Personality:
- Violent and easily alarmed; beats Alice about the face with its wings.
- Full of the deepest contempt for others.
- Anxious, sobbing, and exhausted.
- Sulky when dismissing someone.

Wants:
- To be free of serpents.
- To protect its eggs.
- Alice to be off.

Knows:
- It has tried every way to deal with serpents (roots of trees, banks, hedges), and nothing seems to suit them; "There's no pleasing them!"
- It is hatching eggs and must be on the look-out for serpents night and day.
- It has not had a wink of sleep these three weeks.
- It had taken the highest tree in the wood and thought it would be free of serpents at last, but they came wriggling down from the sky.
- It has seen a good many little girls in its time, but never one with such a neck as Alice's.
- If little girls eat eggs, they are a kind of serpent.
- It does not matter to the Pigeon whether Alice is a little girl or a serpent.

Secret:
- None stated.

Speech:
- Raised voice that rises to a shriek; screams "Serpent!" and repeats it in a more subdued tone with a kind of sob.
- Asks "What are you?" and says Alice is trying to invent something.
- Tone of the deepest contempt.
- Believes Alice is a serpent and says there is no use denying it.
- Asks whether Alice is looking for eggs.
- Sulky when telling Alice to be off.

entities.name: serpents
entities.description: Creatures the Pigeon is bothered by, which come wriggling down from the sky and cannot be pleased by the Pigeon's attempts at roots of trees, banks, or hedges. The Pigeon believes Alice is one of them.

entities.name: highest tree in the wood
entities.description: The highest tree in the wood, taken by the Pigeon as its nest location.

entities.name: tops of the trees
entities.description: Leaves that Alice found to be nothing but the tops of the trees under which she had been wandering.

entities.name: Nest
entities.description: The Pigeon's nest, into which it settled down again.

entities.name: pieces of mushroom
entities.description: Held in Alice's hands. Alice nibbles first at one and then at the other, causing her to grow taller or shorter.

entities.name: beautiful garden
entities.description: Garden Alice wants to get into; how to do so is not yet known to her.

entities.name: open place
entities.description: Open area where Alice came suddenly upon a little house.

entities.name: little house
entities.description: Little house about four feet high, located in an open place. Its occupants are unknown. The door is opened by the Frog-Footman after the Fish-Footman raps on it with his knuckles.

entities.name: wood
entities.description: The wood is near the house. The Fish-Footman ran out of it. Alice crept a little way out of it to listen. She ran back into it when she peeped out, to avoid being heard by the two servants. A small creature trotted quietly into it. Alice later picks her way through it after leaving the tea-party.

entities.name: Fish-Footman
entities.description:
Footman (the first footman, in livery, with powdered hair that curls all over his head). Appears a fish-like face to Alice; he is one of two footmen at the Duchess's door, a Fish-Footman (the one who bears the letter), and also a Frog-Footman, though the text refers to the Frog-Footman as the one who received the letter.

Personality:
- Solemn in tone.
- Bows low.
- Decidedly uncivil in Alice's view: looks up into the sky the whole time he speaks.
- Unaffected by things happening around him (a large plate grazes his nose and he does not react).
- Blunt and dismissive, with a stubborn, slow manner.

Wants:
- To deliver the invitation from the Queen to play croquet, for the Duchess.
- To know whether Alice is to get in at all, which he calls the first question.

Knows:
- The letter is an invitation from the Queen to play croquet, for the Duchess.
- He came running out of the wood and rapped loudly at the door with his knuckles.
- He produced a great letter, nearly as large as himself, from under his arm and handed it to the Frog-Footman.
- There is no use in knocking at the door, for two reasons: first, because he is on the same side of the door as Alice is; secondly, because they are making such a noise inside no one could possibly hear her.
- There might be some sense in knocking if they had the door between them; for instance, if Alice were inside she might knock and he could let her out.
- He shall sit here till tomorrow, or next day maybe.

Secret:
- None stated.

Speech:
- Solemn and formal when delivering messages ("For the Duchess. An invitation from the Queen to play croquet.").
- Speaks to Alice without looking at her, gazing up at the sky.
