- Logical, deadpan reasoning about the door and the noise inside.

entities.name: Frog-Footman
entities.description: Footman in livery with a round face and large eyes like a frog. Opened the door of the little house. Has powdered hair that curls all over his head. Received the great letter and repeated in the same solemn tone, changing the order of the words a little: 'From the Queen. An invitation for the Duchess to play croquet.' Bowed low, and his curls got entangled with the Fish-Footman's.

entities.name: great letter
entities.description: Great letter, nearly as large as the Fish-Footman. An invitation from the Queen to play croquet, addressed for the Duchess.

entities.name: Queen
entities.description:
The Queen of Hearts: sender of the croquet invitation, tyrannical ruler whose court Alice visits, presiding over the croquet game and the trial.

Personality:
- Furious and quick to anger; turns crimson with fury, turns purple when told to hold her tongue, and glares like a wild beast.
- Has only one way of settling all difficulties, great or small: beheading.
- Smiles and passes on after Alice's remark about her.
- Appears with her arms folded, frowning like a thunderstorm.
- Quarrels constantly with the other players.
- Has a shrill voice.
- Was boxed on the ears by the Duchess.
- Her people are dreadfully fond of beheading people.
- Her executions are described by the Gryphon as merely her fancy: they never execute nobody.
- Her last remark made the whole party look grave and anxious.

Wants:
- Has not yet had any dispute with Alice, but it might happen any minute.
- Alice does not like her; she is "extremely likely to win."
- Players of the game are said to quarrel in her presence.

Knows:
- Her arrival is announced by Five with "The Queen! The Queen!", and she is approaching with many footsteps.
- The Rabbit says she can hear whispers nearby.
- Reportedly said only yesterday that Two deserved to be beheaded.
- The gardeners fear she will cut off their heads if she finds the white rose-tree.
- Asks Alice "Have you seen the Mock Turtle yet?"
- Says the Mock Turtle Soup is made from the Mock Turtle.
- Asks what is in the paper found by the White Rabbit.
- Says Alice is nearly two miles high.
- Heard screaming with passion in the distance.
- Argues that if something wasn't done about it in less than no time she'd have everybody executed, all round.
- Remarks that a moment's delay would cost the guests their lives.

Secret:
- Her shrill cries would change to the voice of the shepherd boy.

Speech:
- Shouts "Off with his head!" or "Off with her head!" about once in a minute during the game, often without looking round.
- Screams "Off with her head! Off—"
- Shouts "Get to your places!" in a voice of thunder.
- Orders "Turn them over!" and "Get up!" in a shrill, loud voice.
- Says "Leave off that! You make me giddy."
- Orders "Off with their heads!"
- Asks whether the gardeners' heads are off.
- Asks "Can you play croquet?"
- Roars "Come on, then!" to Alice.
- Shouts a fair warning while stamping on the ground: either the Duchess or her head must be off, in about half no time, and the Duchess must take her choice.
- Says "That proves his guilt."
- Asks "you never had fits, my dear, I think?" (addressed by the King)
- Throws an inkstand at the Lizard while saying "Never!"
- Says "Sentence first—verdict afterwards."
- Shouts "Off with her head!" at the top of her voice.
- Says "No, no!" when the King asks for the jury's verdict.
- Shrieked "Collar that Dormouse! Behead that Dormouse! Turn that Dormouse out of court! Suppress him! Pinch him! Off with his whiskers!"
- Orders "Bring me the list of the singers in the last concert!"
- Ordered an officer to take the Hatter's head off outside the court.
- Ordered the executioner to fetch the Duchess from prison.
- Tells Alice to go on with the game.
- Orders executions and leaves to see after them.
- Shouts "The Queen of Hearts, she made some tarts, All on a summer day" as the accusation (quoted from the verse).

entities.name: other footman
entities.description: A footman who was sitting on the ground near the door, staring stupidly up into the sky when Alice next peeped out. Alice believes perhaps he cannot help looking up, since his eyes are very nearly at the top of his head, but thinks he might at least answer questions.

entities.name: large plate
entities.description: A large plate that came skimming out of the house door straight at the Footman's head, just grazed his nose, and broke to pieces against one of the trees behind him.

entities.name: Footman
entities.description: A footman who stands at the door and speaks in a repetitive, playful manner. Says Alice is 'Are you to get in at all?' and that this is 'the first question'. Says 'I shall sit here, on and off, for days and days.' Says 'Anything you like' when asked what Alice is to do, and then begins whistling. Alice considers him 'perfectly idiotic'.

entities.name: Kitchen
entities.description:
The kitchen is full of smoke. The air contains too much pepper, which causes sneezing. It holds a three-legged stool, a large cauldron of soup, and a hearth with a cat on it.

Alice and the Duchess met here before. The Duchess was savage, possibly because of the pepper.

entities.name: Cook
entities.description:
The Cook: a kitchen cook who stirs a large cauldron of soup over the fire in the Duchess's kitchen.

Personality:
- Leans over the fire, busily stirring the soup.
- Does not sneeze.
- Does not listen to Alice; pays her no attention.
- Violently throws objects at the Duchess and the baby when angered.
- Joins in the chorus of singing.

Knows:
- The Duchess and the baby are in the kitchen with Alice.

Speech:
- Sings along with the chorus: 'Wow! wow! wow!'

entities.name: Baby
entities.description:
The baby, a queer-shaped little creature in the Duchess's household, later said to have turned into a pig.

Appearance:
- Has a very turn-up nose, much more like a snout than a real nose.
- Its eyes are getting extremely small for a baby.
- Has no tears.
- Is a queer-shaped little creature that holds out its arms and legs in all directions.
- Has a nose that nearly got carried off by an unusually large saucepan.

Personality:
- Sneezes and howls alternately without a moment's pause.
- Is howling so much that it is impossible to say whether the blows hurt it or not.
- Howls while the Duchess sings the second verse and is tossed up and down.
- Snorts like a steam-engine when Alice catches it, and keeps doubling itself up and straightening itself out again.
- Sneezed at first but had left off sneezing by the time Alice speaks of murder.
- Grunts and sobs, and it is impossible to say which.
- Turns into a pig, which Alice realizes by its violent grunting.

Knows:
- Is nursed by the Duchess in the kitchen.
- Is being struck by thrown objects.
- Is the Duchess's child.
- Is a baby that Alice is nursing and carrying.
- According to Alice, turned into a pig.
- The Cat asks what became of it.

entities.name: Cheshire cat
entities.description:
The Cheshire Cat: a large cat with a continual grin, found sitting on the kitchen hearth, on a tree bough, as a grin in the air, as a head appearing before the body, and in the Queen's court.

Personality:
- Good-natured in appearance, but has very long claws and a great many teeth.
- Grins continually; the Duchess states it grins because it is a Cheshire cat.
- Does not sneeze.
- Only grinned when it saw Alice, and grinned a little wider when addressed as 'Cheshire Puss'.
- Cryptic and playful, speaking in riddles about direction and destination.
- Disliked by the King's look; the King looks at it with great curiosity.
- Remarks 'I'd rather not' when the King asks it to kiss his hand.

Wants:
- Wants Alice to decide where she wants to get to; claims it doesn't matter which way she goes if she has no destination.

Knows:
- Cats that always grin: the Duchess says all cats can grin and most do; Alice says she knows of none that do.
- A Hatter lives in the direction its right paw points, and a March Hare lives in the direction of its other paw.
- Visiting either the Hatter or the March Hare is fine, because both are mad.
- Alice will get somewhere "if you only walk long enough."
- "We're all mad here. I'm mad. You're mad."
- "You must be, or you wouldn't have come here."

Secret:
- Its appearance is subject to shifting: it appears as a grin in the air, and the head appears first, with eyes before ears, the whole head appearing in sight after a minute.
- Seems to think there is enough of the game in sight and no more of it appears.
- Its removal is requested by the King; a large crowd gathers around it when Alice returns.

Speech:
- Speaks once there is enough mouth for it to speak with.
- Speaks in a low voice when asking how Alice likes the Queen.
- Asks "How are you getting on?" as soon as there is mouth enough to speak, and asked it again as a grin in the air.
- Says "That depends a good deal on where you want to get to" and "Then it doesn't matter which way you go."
- Says "I'm mad. You're mad" and "We're all mad here."

entities.name: Soup
entities.description: Contained in a large cauldron, stirred by the cook over the fire. Has too much pepper in it, according to Alice.

entities.name: Three-legged stool
entities.description: A stool in the middle of the kitchen on which the Duchess sits.

entities.name: cauldron of soup
entities.description: Taken off the fire by the cook.

entities.name: fire-irons
entities.description: Thrown by the cook at the Duchess and the baby; they came first.

entities.name: saucepans
entities.description: Thrown by the cook at the Duchess and the baby in a shower after the fire-irons.

entities.name: plates
entities.description: Thrown by the cook at the Duchess and the baby in a shower with saucepans and dishes.

entities.name: dishes
entities.description: Thrown by the cook at the Duchess and the baby in a shower with saucepans and plates.

entities.name: unusually large saucepan
entities.description: Flew close by the baby's nose and very nearly carried it off.

entities.name: earth
entities.description: Takes twenty-four hours to turn round on its axis, according to Alice.

entities.name: Frying-pan
entities.description: Thrown by the cook after the Duchess as she leaves; it just misses her.

entities.name: Lullaby
entities.description: A song the Duchess sings to her child. Verse one: 'Speak roughly to your little boy, And beat him when he sneezes: He only does it to annoy, Because he knows it teases.' Verse two: 'I speak severely to my boy, I beat him when he sneezes; For he can thoroughly enjoy The pepper when he pleases!' Chorus: 'Wow! wow! wow!' (sung with the cook and the baby).

entities.name: Croquet game
entities.description: A game of croquet that the Duchess must go and get ready to play with the Queen.

entities.name: The Room
entities.description: The unnamed room where the Duchess nursed the baby, sang the lullaby, and handed the baby to Alice. The Duchess hurries out of it.

entities.name: open air
entities.description: The outdoor area where Alice carries the baby after nursing it.

entities.name: little creature
entities.description: A small creature that was once a baby, which Alice set down. It trotted away quietly into the wood. Alice described it as a rather handsome pig, and said it would have been a dreadfully ugly child if it had grown up.

entities.name: Hatter
entities.description:
The Mad Hatter, a mad person who lives in the direction the Cheshire Cat indicated with its right paw. Visiting him is optional, as the Cat said he is mad. He is found having tea at the table under a tree in front of the March Hare's house, with the March Hare and the Dormouse.

Personality:
- Mad, and the Cheshire Cat said so.
- Curious; had been looking at Alice for some time with great curiosity.
- Rude; says Alice's hair wants cutting.
- Opens his eyes very wide on hearing Alice's rebuke about personal remarks.
- Rude and dismissive; tells Alice "Then you shouldn't talk," and his rudeness is more than Alice can bear.
- Uses the Dormouse as a cushion, resting his elbows on it and talking over its head.
- Mournful in tone, speaking with a sigh.
- Tosses his head contemptuously.
- Nervous and wretched as a witness; shifts from foot to foot, looks uneasily at the Queen, turns pale and fidgets when the Queen stares at him.
- Trembles so much at the Queen's order that he shook both his shoes off.
- Anxious; looks anxiously around to see if the March Hare will deny what he has said.
- Triumphant when he asks "Who's making personal remarks now?"

Wants:
- A clean cup: "I want a clean cup."
- Everyone to move one place on: "let's all move one place on." He moves on as he speaks and is the only one who gets any advantage from the change of places.
- To finish his tea: "I'd rather finish my tea."

Knows:
- Asks "Why is a raven like a writing-desk?"
- Says "Not the same thing a bit!"
- Says "You might just as well say that 'I see what I eat' is the same thing as 'I eat what I see'!"
- Says "It is the same thing with you."
- Asks Alice "What day of the month is it?" as the first to break the silence.
- His watch tells only the day of the month; he muttered "Why should it?" about this.
- Asks "Does your watch tell you what year it is?" and says his watch is the same case: "Which is just the case with mine."
- Has taken his watch out of his pocket, looks at it uneasily, shakes it every now and then, and holds it to his ear.
- Sighs "Two days wrong!" and angrily tells the March Hare "I told you butter wouldn't suit the works!"
- Grumbles that some crumbs must have got in as well and that the March Hare shouldn't have put it in with the bread-knife.
- Pours a little hot tea upon the Dormouse's nose to wake it.
- Asks whether Alice has guessed the riddle yet. He has no idea of the answer.
- Says that if Alice knew Time as well as he does, she wouldn't talk about wasting it.
- Speaks of Time as if he knows it well, and says Time "won't stand beating."
- Believes that if one keeps on good terms with Time, Time would do almost anything one likes with the clock: whispering a hint to Time makes the clock go round in a twinkling (e.g., nine o'clock in the morning, just time to begin lessons, becomes half-past one, time for dinner).
- Says one could keep it to half-past one as long as one liked.
- Says he and Time quarrelled last March, just before the March Hare "went mad," at the great concert given by the Queen of Hearts.
- At that concert he had to sing "Twinkle, twinkle, little bat! How I wonder what you're at!" He knows the song continues: "Up above the world you fly, Like a tea-tray in the sky. Twinkle, twinkle—"
- He had hardly finished the first verse when the Queen jumped up and bawled out, "He's murdering the time! Off with his head!"
- Since then the March Hare won't do a thing he asks, and it's always six o'clock now.
- It's always tea-time, they have no time to wash the things between whiles, and the things are kept moving round as they get used up.
- The Dormouse was asleep and was pinched on both sides at once to wake up.
- Shakes his head mournfully when asked if he manages time that way.
- Holds a teaspoon.
- Says "You mean you can't take less," and that it's very easy to take more than nothing.
- Suggests "You can draw water out of a water-well... so I should think you could draw treacle out of a treacle-well—eh, stupid?"
- Pinches the Dormouse, which makes it wake with a little shriek.
- Attends a tea-party with Alice, the Dormouse, and others; the last time Alice saw them they were trying to put the Dormouse into the teapot.
- As a witness, came in with a teacup in one hand and a piece of bread-and-butter in the other. Apologized for bringing these in, saying he hadn't quite finished his tea when he was sent for.
- Says he began on "Fourteenth of March, I think it was."
- Says "It isn't mine" about the hat. Says "I keep them to sell; I've none of my own. I'm a hatter."
- Bit a large piece out of his teacup instead of the bread-and-butter.
- Says he cut bread-and-butter and that most things twinkled after that.
- Accuses the March Hare of saying something about the Dormouse, but cannot remember what the Dormouse said: "That I can't remember."
- Dropped his teacup and bread-and-butter and went down on one knee, saying "I'm a poor man, your Majesty." Says "I can't go no lower: I'm on the floor, as it is."
- Was dismissed by the King and hurriedly left the court without even waiting to put his shoes on. The Queen ordered that his head be taken off outside, but he was out of sight before the officer could reach the door.

Secret:
- Says "It's him" when asked about the riddle's answer.

Speech:
- Mournful, with sighs.
- Repeats "I'm a poor man" and "It began with the tea."
- Full quotes include: "Not the same thing a bit!", "Then you shouldn't talk", "I want a clean cup", "Be quick about it, or you'll be asleep again before it's done", and "I'm a poor man, your Majesty... I hadn't begun my tea—not above a week or so—and what with the bread-and-butter getting so thin—and the twinkling of the tea—".

entities.name: March Hare
entities.description:
The March Hare, a mad host of the tea party, who lives in a large house with chimneys shaped like ears and a roof thatched with fur.

Personality:
- Mad; said to be raving mad in March, though Alice thinks he may be less mad in May.
- Offers wine encouragingly, but admits there is none.
- Stubbornly insists "It was the best butter, you know."
- Meekly says "It was the best butter."
- Looks gloomily at the watch, dips it into his cup of tea, and looks at it again.
- Could think of nothing better to say than his first remark.
- Interrupts in a great hurry, and denies accusations with "I deny it!"

Wants:
- To interrupt yawning and change the subject, because he is getting tired of this.
- To vote that the young lady tells a story.
- To have the Dormouse tell a story.
- Alice to say what she means.

Knows:
- Lives in the direction the Cheshire Cat indicated with its other paw; visiting him is optional, as the Cat said he is mad.
- Said to live in the direction Alice walks, which Alice believes will be much the most interesting.
- Lives in a large house whose chimneys are shaped like ears and whose roof is thatched with fur.
- Sits at a table under a tree in front of the house, having tea with the Hatter.
- Uses the Dormouse as a cushion, resting his elbows on it and talking over its head.
- Went mad, according to the Hatter, shortly after the quarrel with Time last March.
- Moves into the Dormouse's place when the company changes seats.
- Upset the milk-jug into his plate.
- Followed the Hatter into the court, arm-in-arm with the Dormouse.
- Says the Hatter began on 'Fifteenth'.
- Shares a never-ending meal with his friends, from which the rattle of teacups is heard.
- Is pointed at with a tea spoon by the Hatter.
- Wakes the Dormouse by pinching it on both sides at once, together with the Hatter.

Secret:
- None stated.

Speech:
- "No room! No room!" (when Alice came)
- "There isn't any."
- "It wasn't very civil of you to sit down without being invited." Says it was not very civil of Alice to sit down without being invited.
- Says Alice should say what she means.
- "You might just as well say, that 'I like what I get' is the same thing as 'I get what I like'!"
- "It was the best butter, you know."
- Said to Alice, very earnestly, "Take some more tea."
- "Sh! sh!" (said together with the Hatter to quiet Alice)
- "Nor I" (when asked about the riddle's answer)
- "Why not?" (when Alice asks why the drawings begin with an M)
- 'I only wish it was' (said to itself in a whisper, referring to half-past one, time for dinner)
- "I didn't!" (interrupting in a great hurry)
- "I deny it!"

entities.name: bough of a tree
entities.description: A bough of a tree a few yards off from Alice, where the Cheshire Cat sat.

entities.name: croquet
entities.description: A game of croquet to be played with the Queen today. Alice has not been invited yet.

entities.name: branch of a tree
entities.description: A branch of a tree where the Cat is seen sitting.

entities.name: grin
entities.description: The Cat's grin, which remained visible for some time after the rest of the Cat had vanished. Alice found a grin without a cat curious.

entities.name: Dormouse
entities.description:
A sleepy, drowsy creature (the Dormouse) seated at the tea-party between the March Hare and the Hatter, often used as a cushion by them.

Personality:
- Falls asleep instantly and constantly; drowsy, yawns and rubs its eyes because it is getting very sleepy.
- Claims it was never asleep and heard every word, even when plainly dozing.
- Sulky when pressed; remarks "If you can't be civil, you'd better finish the story for yourself."
- Indignant when corrected; replies "One, indeed!"
- Speaks in a hoarse, feeble voice.

Wants:
- Wants to be left alone to sleep, and to be treated civilly.

Knows:
- Says the Hatter began on 'Sixteenth'.
- Claims the story "Once upon a time there were three little sisters", whose names were Elsie, Lacie, and Tillie, lived at the bottom of a well.
- Says the sisters lived on treacle, after thinking a minute or two; admits the sisters were very ill, since they couldn't have lived on treacle.
- Says "It was a treacle-well."
- Answers that the creatures were 'in the well'—'well in'.
- Says the sisters were learning to draw and drew all manner of things that begin with an M, such as mouse-traps, the moon, memory, and muchness.
- Says things are 'much of a muchness' and asks Alice if she ever saw a drawing of a muchness.
- Says "I breathe when I sleep" is the same as "I sleep when I breathe" (said in its sleep: "You might just as well say, that 'I breathe when I sleep' is the same thing as 'I sleep when I breathe'!").
- Answers "Treacle" without considering at all, when asked what tarts are made of, from behind the cook.

Secret:
- Was being put into the teapot by the Hatter and others the last time Alice saw them.

Speech:
- Mumbles in sleep, with lines such as "Of course, of course; just what I was going to remark myself."
- Hoarse and feeble when awake; sulky and indignant when interrupted.
- Answers quickly and bluntly, such as "Treacle," with little thought.

entities.name: house of the March Hare
entities.description: A very large house in front of which a table is set out under a tree. Its chimneys are shaped like ears and its roof is thatched with fur.

entities.name: table under tree
entities.description: A large table set out under a tree in front of the March Hare's house. Crowded at one corner by the March Hare, the Hatter and the Dormouse. Has nothing on it but tea.

entities.name: large arm-chair
entities.description: Large arm-chair at one end of the table, in which Alice sat down.

entities.name: tea
entities.description: The March Hare and the Hatter were having tea. It was the only thing on the table. The March Hare offered some to Alice, saying, "Take some more tea." Alice helped herself to some.

entities.name: lefthand bit of mushroom
entities.description: A piece of mushroom; Alice nibbled some of it to raise herself to about two feet high.

entities.name: A Mad Tea-Party
entities.description: Chapter VII. The tea party held at the table under a tree in front of the March Hare's house, attended by the March Hare, the Hatter, the Dormouse and Alice.

entities.name: riddle: Why is a raven like a writing-desk?
entities.description: A riddle asked by the Hatter. Alice claims she can guess it; the answer is not given in the text.

entities.name: Party
entities.description: The gathering at the table of Alice, the March Hare, the Hatter and the Dormouse, which sits silent for a minute after the conversation drops.

entities.name: butter
entities.description: Described by the March Hare as the best butter; the Hatter said it would not suit the works and that it was put in with the bread-knife.

entities.name: riddle
entities.description: A riddle that Alice gave up on; the Hatter and March Hare have no answer to it. Alice says riddles that have no answers are a waste of time.

entities.name: Time
entities.description:
Time

Personality:
- Personified as a male figure ("him") by the Hatter.
- Does not like being beaten ("He won't stand beating").

Wants:
- Good terms with those who wish to change the clock; he can be made to change it if one keeps on good terms with him.

Knows:
- The Hatter claims to know Time well.
- Wasting time is wasting him, according to the Hatter.
- The Hatter quarrelled with him last March.

Speech:
- Referred to by the Hatter as 'him' ("It's him.").

entities.name: Queen of Hearts
entities.description:
Queen of Hearts, a short-tempered monarch who sits on the throne beside the King of Hearts.

Personality:
- Quick to anger and bursts out in rage at small provocations

Wants:
- Has the Hatter's head removed for any perceived offense

Knows:
- Gave the great concert last March, where the Hatter had to sing
- Was seated on the throne together with the King of Hearts when Alice arrived

Speech:
- Shouts commands and threats, such as "He's murdering the time! Off with his head!"

entities.name: clock
entities.description: Can be made to go round in a twinkling by Time, if one keeps on good terms with him, e.g., from nine o'clock in the morning to half-past one.

entities.name: great concert
entities.description: Concert given by the Queen of Hearts last March, at which the Hatter had to sing 'Twinkle, twinkle, little bat!'. The quarrel with Time happened there.

entities.name: Twinkle, twinkle, little bat song
entities.description: Song sung by the Hatter at the great concert: 'Twinkle, twinkle, little bat! How I wonder what you're at!' Continues: 'Up above the world you fly, Like a tea-tray in the sky. Twinkle, twinkle—'.

entities.name: tea spoon
entities.description: Held by the Hatter, who points with it at the March Hare.

entities.name: Elsie
entities.description: One of three little sisters in the Dormouse's story, who lived at the bottom of a well and lived on treacle, and was very ill.

entities.name: Lacie
entities.description: One of three little sisters in the Dormouse's story, who lived at the bottom of a well and lived on treacle, and was very ill.

entities.name: Tillie
entities.description: One of three little sisters in the Dormouse's story, who lived at the bottom of a well and lived on treacle, and was very ill.

entities.name: tea-things
entities.description: Many are put out at the tea-time table. Are kept moving round as they get used up, and there is no time to wash them between whiles.

entities.name: treacle
entities.description:
The Dormouse says the three little sisters lived on treacle. Alice says they would have been ill from it.

Treacle is a substance the Dormouse mentions first. Alice asks where it was drawn from. The Hatter suggests it could be drawn out of a treacle-well.

entities.name: three little sisters
entities.description: Lived at the bottom of a well, which was a treacle-well. Were learning to draw, and drew treacle.

entities.name: treacle-well
entities.description: The three little sisters lived at the bottom of a well, according to the Dormouse. The Hatter suggests treacle could be drawn from a well. Alice says they were in the well.

entities.name: bread-and-butter
entities.description: Alice helped herself to some bread-and-butter. It was the bread-and-butter the Hatter should have bitten instead of his teacup. It was so thin. The Hatter cut it and dropped it along with his teacup.

entities.name: clean cup
entities.description: The Hatter wants a clean cup.

entities.name: milk-jug
entities.description: A jug of milk that the March Hare upset into his plate.

entities.name: water-well
entities.description: A well from which water can be drawn, according to the Hatter's comparison.

entities.name: The Tea-Party
entities.description: A tea-party Alice attended with the Hatter and the Dormouse; Alice calls it 'the stupidest tea-party I ever was at in all my life!'. Alice leaves it in great disgust.

entities.name: Tree with door
entities.description: One of the trees has a door leading right into it; Alice goes in at once.

entities.name: Little glass table
entities.description: A little glass table located in the long hall.

entities.name: Little passage
entities.description: A little passage Alice walks down to reach the garden.

entities.name: The Queen's Croquet-Ground
entities.description: Chapter VIII setting; the garden where a large rose-tree stands near the entrance.

entities.name: Large rose-tree
entities.description: Stands near the entrance of the garden; its roses are white, and three gardeners are busily painting them red.

entities.name: Five
entities.description:
Gardener in the Queen's garden, one of three painting the roses red. Sulky in manner, and anxious about the Queen's approach.

Personality:
- Sulky in tone
- Anxious; watches across the garden and calls out in alarm

Wants:
- Not to be blamed for the spilled paint

Knows:
- Says Two was to be beheaded for bringing the cook tulip-roots instead of onions
- Says he heard the Queen say only yesterday that Two deserved to be beheaded

Secret:
- None stated

Speech:
- Says "I couldn't help it"
- Says "Seven jogged my elbow."
- Calls out "The Queen! The Queen!"
- Blames Seven for jogging his elbow
- Told by a gardener to "Look out now, Five! Don't go splashing paint over me like that!"

entities.name: Seven
entities.description:
One of the three gardeners painting the roses red, a card-gardener in Wonderland.

Personality:
- Quick to blame others and quick to take offence.
- Checks himself when his eye falls on Alice.

Wants:
- Not stated.

Knows:
- Five always lays the blame on others.
- Two's punishment is none of his business (he tells Two this).

Secret:
- Not stated.

Speech:
- Says "That's right, Five! Always lay the blame on others!"
- Begins "Well, of all the unjust things—" and then checks himself when his eye falls on Alice.

entities.name: Three gardeners
entities.description:
Three gardeners paint the white roses of a large rose-tree red. Five and Seven are among them.

The gardeners are flat and oblong, with hands and feet at the corners. They lie on their faces around the rose-tree. Their backs show the same pattern as the rest of the pack, so you cannot tell if they are gardeners, soldiers, courtiers, or the Queen's children.

Gardeners tend the rose-tree. When told to rise, they jump up and bow to the King, the Queen, the royal children, and everyone else. One, called Two, kneels humbly and says, "we were trying—". They run to Alice for protection, and she hides them in a large flower-pot. The Queen sentences them to be beheaded.

entities.name: White roses
entities.description: Roses growing on the large rose-tree; they were white and are being painted red by the gardeners.

entities.name: Two
entities.description:
Gardener (one of three gardeners who paint the roses in the Queen's garden)

Personality:
- Very humble; speaks in a low voice
- Frightened of the Queen and of being beheaded

Wants:
- To avoid execution by beheading
- Ensure the rose-tree is fixed before the Queen arrives

Knows:
- The rose-tree ought to have been a red rose-tree
- They put a white one in by mistake
- If the Queen finds out, they will all have their heads cut off
- They are doing their best before she comes

Speech:
- Very humble tone, going down on one knee
- Begins with "May it please your Majesty, we were trying—"

entities.name: brush
entities.description: Belongs to Seven; he flings it down upon being interrupted by Alice's presence.

entities.name: tulip-roots
entities.description: Were brought to the cook by Two instead of onions, which was given as the reason for his beheading.

entities.name: soldiers
entities.description:
Ten soldiers, oblong and flat like the three gardeners, with hands and feet at the corners.

Knows:
- They came first in the procession, carrying clubs.
- They were shaped like the three gardeners, oblong and flat, with their hands and feet at the corners.
- They walked two and two.
- They must double themselves up and stand on their hands and feet to make the arches for the croquet game.
- They take those sentenced by the Queen into custody, and had to leave off being arches to do this.
- Two of them stand on each side of the Knave to guard him.

entities.name: courtiers
entities.description: Ten courtiers who came after the soldiers. Ornamented all over with diamonds, and walked two and two, as the soldiers did.

entities.name: royal children
entities.description:
Ten royal children who came after the courtiers, jumping merrily along hand in hand, in couples, ornamented with hearts. Also a member of the royal family mentioned among those the gardeners bow to.

Personality:
- Merry and playful (jumping merrily along)

Knows:
- The gardeners bow to them (as a member of the royal family)

entities.name: guests
entities.description: Guests who came next in the procession, mostly Kings and Queens.

entities.name: Knave of Hearts
entities.description:
The Knave of Hearts, a servant-like figure who carries the King's crown in a royal procession.

Personality:
- Bows and smiles politely when addressed.

Knows:
- Carries the King's crown on a crimson velvet cushion.
- Named in the accusation: "The Knave of Hearts, he stole those tarts, And took them quite away!"

Speech:
- No spoken lines recorded; replies to the Queen's question "Who is this?" with a bow and a smile.

entities.name: King and Queen of Hearts
entities.description: Came last of all in the grand procession. The Queen said severely 'Who is this?' upon stopping opposite Alice, and called Alice 'child' while tossing her head impatiently at the Knave of Hearts' non-answer, calling him 'Idiot!'. The Queen asked Alice what her name was and pointed to the three gardeners lying round the rose-tree, asking who they were.

entities.name: rose-tree
entities.description: Three gardeners lie around a rose-tree. The Queen examines the roses on it, which the gardeners tend.

entities.name: King's crown
entities.description: Carried by the Knave of Hearts on a crimson velvet cushion.

entities.name: crimson velvet cushion
entities.description: Crimson velvet cushion on which the Knave of Hearts carried the King's crown.

entities.name: King
entities.description:
A king presiding over the court. He wears spectacles, which he puts on to make out who is talking, and the three gardeners bow to him.

Personality:
- Timid and anxious; he gently pleads for Alice when she is only a child.
- Very decided that the Cat must be removed.
- Angry and sharp with witnesses, threatening execution at the slightest provocation.
- Melancholy when reluctantly giving in, and grave in his speech.
- Offended when his puns or words are questioned, and relieved by turns.
- Easily confused and flustered, often pale and trembling when startled.

Wants:
- The Cat removed; he calls the Queen and asks her to have the cat removed.
- To fetch the executioner himself, and eagerly offers to do so.
- The trial to proceed: he demands evidence from witnesses and asks the jury to consider their verdict.
- The jury back in their proper places before the trial can proceed.

Knows:
- Alice is only a child.
- The Cat's head disappeared, and he ran wildly up and down looking for it.
- Anything that had a head could be beheaded.
- He calls the verses the most important piece of evidence heard yet.
- He interprets "We know it to be true" as referring to the jury, and "I gave her one, they gave him two" as what the Knave did with the tarts.
- Rule Forty-two: "All persons more than a mile high to leave the court."
- The rule is the oldest rule in the book.
- Twinkling begins with a T.
- Tarts are made of something he asks about: "What are tarts made of?"
- He asks the Knave whether he can swim.
- He asks the Queen whether she ever had fits, as he thinks she has not.
- The Dormouse was one of the players not taken into custody during the game.
- The verses were not in the prisoner's handwriting, so the prisoner "must have imitated somebody else's hand."
- The Knave did not sign the verses, which makes the matter worse; the Knave must have meant some mischief.
- The verses are written to nobody, which isn't usual.
- He spreads the verses on his knee and looks at them with one eye while muttering to himself.
- He thinks the verses may have no meaning, which would save a world of trouble, but then seems to see some meaning in them after all.
- He claims that "Then the words don't fit you" is a pun.
- He says "Let the jury consider their verdict" for about the twentieth time that day.
- He mutters to himself "important—unimportant—unimportant—important—" as if trying which word sounds best.
- His remark about the signature was the first really clever thing he said that day, which earned a general clapping of hands.

Secret:
- He is uncertain of the words he chooses, and tries different ones to see which sounds best.

Speech:
- "Consider, my dear: she is only a child!"
- "You are all pardoned."
- "Herald, read the accusation!"
- "Consider your verdict."
- "Call the first witness."
- "Write that down."
- "Take off your hat."
- "Stolen!"
- "You ought to have finished."
- "When did you begin?"
- "Give your evidence."
- "Don't be nervous, or I'll have you executed on the spot."
- "Give your evidence... or I'll have you executed, whether you're nervous or not."
- "The twinkling of the what?"
- "Of course twinkling begins with a T!"
- "Do you take me for a dunce? Go on!"
- "He denies it, leave out that part."
- "You _must_ remember, or I'll have you executed."
- "You're a _very_ poor _speaker_."
- "If that's all you know about it, you may stand down."
- "Then you may sit down."
- "You may go."
- "Call the next witness!"
- "Collar that Dormouse."
- "Well, if I must, I must."
- "Never mind!"
- "Really, my dear, you must cross-examine the next witness. It quite makes my forehead ache!"
- "The trial cannot proceed until all the jurymen are back in their proper places—all."
- "That's very important."
- "Silence!"
- "Rule Forty-two. All persons more than a mile high to leave the court."
- "Consider their verdict."
- "Un_important, of course, I meant."
- "It must have been that."
- "Unless it was written to nobody, which isn't usual, you know."
- "If you didn't sign it, that only makes the matter worse. You must have meant some mischief, or else you'd have signed your name like an honest man."
- "Read them."
- "Begin at the beginning, and go on till you come to the end: then stop."
- "Then the words don't fit you."
- "It's a pun!"

entities.name: Knave
entities.description:
Card character in the court of the King and Queen of Hearts; made entirely of cardboard. Stands before the King and Queen in chains, with a soldier on each side to guard him, while on trial.

Knows:
- Turns the gardeners over very carefully, with one foot, on the Queen's order.
- Is accused of writing the verses.
- There is no name signed at the end of the verses.

Speech:
- "Please your Majesty, I didn't write it, and they can't prove I did: there's no name signed at the end."
- When asked whether he can swim, shakes his head sadly and says 'Do I look like it?'.

entities.name: three soldiers
entities.description: Soldiers who remain behind to execute the gardeners; wander about looking for the gardeners in the flower-pot, then quietly march off; shout 'Their heads are gone, if it please your Majesty!' in reply to the Queen; are silent and look at Alice when asked about croquet.

entities.name: large flower-pot
entities.description: Large flower-pot standing near; Alice puts the three gardeners into it for protection.

entities.name: procession
entities.description: Procession that moves on with the Queen, the King, and soldiers; Alice joins it.

entities.name: Croquet-ground
entities.description:
The croquet-ground is curious and full of ridges and furrows. Balls are live hedgehogs. Mallets are live flamingoes. Soldiers must double themselves up and stand on their hands and feet to make the arches.

This is the place where the game is played. The Queen and Alice return here to continue the game. The other guests are also here.

entities.name: Live hedgehogs
entities.description: Used as balls in the croquet game on the croquet-ground.

entities.name: Live flamingoes
entities.description: Used as mallets in the croquet game on the croquet-ground.

entities.name: Game of croquet
entities.description: Began after people got settled down in a minute or two following the Queen's shout; played on the croquet-ground.

entities.name: flamingo
entities.description:
Alice's flamingo is used as a croquet mallet. Its body tucks under her arm, legs hanging down, but its neck tends to twist round. It looks up with a puzzled expression. Its head is used to strike the hedgehog.

Alice puts it down to begin an account of the game. It once flew off across the garden, trying to reach a tree. Alice caught it, brought it back, and tucked it under her arm so it would not escape again.

Its temper is doubtful, according to the Duchess. Alice thinks it might bite.

entities.name: hedgehog
entities.description:
Hedgehogs are used as balls in the game. They often unroll and crawl away. Players fight over them.

The Queen's hedgehog ran away when it saw Alice's coming. Alice would have croqueted it. Like everything in the game, it is alive.

Alice's hedgehog is used as a croquet mallet. It fought another hedgehog and is now out of sight.

entities.name: doubled-up soldiers
entities.description: Soldiers who are doubled up and are always getting up and walking off to other parts of the ground, serving as hoops in the game.

entities.name: the ground
entities.description: The playing field has ridges or furrows. Soldiers walk doubled up across it. Hedgehogs are sent across it. The arch is at its other end.

entities.name: game
entities.description: This is a game with no clear rules. Players quarrel and do not play fair. The game is confusing, and Alice never knows whether it is her turn. Living things are used as equipment, including hedgehogs and flamingos for croquet. Alice describes the game to the Cat. After the Cat's head disappears, the party returns to the game. Alice says the game is going better now.

entities.name: arch
entities.description: Alice has to go through it next; it is walking about at the other end of the ground.

entities.name: executioner
entities.description:
Persona: The Executioner

A man fetched by the King to carry out executions, who takes part in a dispute among the King, the Queen, and himself, all talking at once.

Personality:
- Argumentative, and willing to voice his objection to the Queen's and King's demands.
- Feels his age and refuses to take up a new kind of work at this stage of his life.
- Prompt and eager to act when sent on an errand.

Wants:
- Not to be made to behead someone when there is no body to sever the head from.
- Not to begin a practice he has never had to do before.

Knows:
- Was sent by the Queen to fetch the Duchess from prison.
- Went off like an arrow on that errand.
- You cannot cut off a head unless there is a body to cut it off from.

Speech:
- Argues his point in a stubborn, reasoned way, appealing to logic about what can and cannot be done.
- Mentions his time of life as a reason for refusing.

entities.name: other hedgehog
entities.description: Engaged in a fight with Alice's hedgehog; out of sight when Alice returns.

entities.name: players
entities.description:
Players of the game in Wonderland's croquet match, a group of silent figures who look very uncomfortable at the dispute.

Personality:
- Quite silent.
- Looks very uncomfortable at the dispute.

Wants:
- Nothing stated.

Knows:
- Three of them were sentenced by the Queen to be executed for having missed their turns.
- Those sentenced were taken into custody and placed under sentence of execution, except the King, the Queen, and Alice.

Secret:
- Nothing stated.

Speech:
- Nothing stated.

entities.name: crowd
entities.description:
A quite large crowd that gathered round the Cheshire Cat when Alice returns. The crowd below is the group onto whose heads the jurymen were upset when Alice tipped over the jury-box.

Personality:
- All the rest are quite silent and look very uncomfortable.

Knows:
- A quite large crowd collected round the Cheshire Cat when Alice returns.
- The jurymen were upset onto the heads of the crowd below when Alice tipped over the jury-box.

entities.name: dispute
entities.description: A dispute going on between the executioner, the King, and the Queen, who are all talking at once, around the Cheshire Cat.

entities.name: Cat's head
entities.description: Began fading away and entirely disappeared before the executioner returned with the Duchess; the King and executioner ran wildly up and down looking for it.

entities.name: Mock Turtle's Story
entities.description: Title of Chapter IX.

entities.name: prison
entities.description: Place where the Duchess was being held before being fetched by the executioner.

entities.name: pepper
entities.description: Spice believed by Alice to make people hot-tempered; Alice thinks it made the Duchess savage when they met in the kitchen.

entities.name: mustard
entities.description: Said to bite, according to the Duchess. Not a bird, according to Alice. Described by Alice as a mineral at first and then as a vegetable that does not look like one.

entities.name: mustard-mine
entities.description: A large mustard-mine said by the Duchess to be near here.

entities.name: other guests
entities.description: Had taken advantage of the Queen's absence and were resting in the shade. When they see the Queen, they hurry back to the game, because the Queen remarked that a moment's delay would cost them their lives.

entities.name: shade
entities.description: Shaded area where the other guests rested during the Queen's absence.

entities.name: Mock Turtle
entities.description:
Mock Turtle: a sad, lonely creature made from the Mock Turtle Soup, with a history the Gryphon tells Alice; sits on a little ledge of rock in the distance, with large eyes full of tears.

Personality:
- Sad and lonely; sighs as if his heart would break and sobs heavily.
- Becomes angry and calls Alice "really very dull!"
- Thoughtful; repeats that "It all came different!"
- Anxious when asking Alice about her school.
- Offended when misunderstood: "I mean what I say."
- Sighs deeply, draws the back of one flapper across his eyes, tears running down his cheeks; his voice is choked by sobs at times.
- Jumps about like a mad thing before sitting down sadly and quietly.
- Yawns and shuts his eyes while speaking.
- Hides his face in his paws with the Gryphon at one point.
- Sighs deeply before singing.
- Miserable; in the sister's dream, his distant sobs would in reality be replaced by the lowing of the cattle in the distance.

Wants:
- Tells Alice and the Gryphon to sit down and not speak until he has finished.
- Wants to hear Alice try to repeat something, and tells the Gryphon to tell her to begin.
- Wants the verse explained.
- Persists in asking about the Lobster's toes and how he could turn them out with his nose.
- Offers to show Alice a little of the dance: "We can do without lobsters, you know."
- Asks which of them shall sing.
- Asks the Gryphon to tell Alice about the reason and all that.
- Asks Alice to explain all that.

Knows:
- He was called Tortoise by the speaker's group because the master, an old Turtle, taught them; "We called him Tortoise because he taught us."
- They went to school in the sea, went to school every day, and had the best of educations.
- His school had "French, music, and washing—extra" at the end of the bill.
- He could not afford extras and only took the regular course: Reeling and Writhing to begin with, then the branches of Arithmetic: Ambition, Distraction, Uglification, and Derision.
- "Uglify" means "to make anything prettier" in the sense of Alice's first definition.
- His lessons included Mystery (ancient and modern), with Seaography, then Drawling, Stretching, and Fainting in Coils, taught by the Drawling-master.
- He cannot show Drawling himself because he is too stiff, and the Gryphon never learnt it.
- He never went to the Classics master, who taught Laughing and Grief, as they used to say.
- He had ten hours of lessons the first day, nine the next, and so on; the eleventh day must have been a holiday, "Of course it was."
- The Lobster Quadrille is a delightful thing: form two lines, seals, turtles, and salmon, and so on; clear all the jelly-fish out of the way; advance twice; set to partners; change lobsters and retire in same order; throw the lobsters as far out to sea as you can; turn a somersault in the sea while capering wildly about; back to land again, which ends the first figure.
- "You may not have lived much under the sea," and "perhaps you were never even introduced to a lobster."
- Crumbs would all wash off in the sea; Alice is wrong about the crumbs.
- The whiting have their tails in their mouths, and the reason is cut off by a yawn; he doesn't know where Dinn may be.
- "They were obliged to have him with them" about the porpoise; "no wise fish would go anywhere without a porpoise."
- If a fish came to him and said he was going a journey, he would say "With what porpoise?"
- Sings the song about the whiting very slowly and sadly, and speaks of the whiting as something Alice has presumably seen ("they—you've seen them, of course?").
- He has never heard the verse before; it "sounds uncommon nonsense."
- Sings "Turtle Soup" with the song "Beautiful Soup" as its performance, in a voice sometimes choked with sobs.
- Interrupts to complain that repeating verses without explaining them is "by far the most confusing thing" it ever heard.
- Says he has no sorrow according to the Gryphon's claim, which the Gryphon calls "his fancy."
- Had just begun to repeat the Gryphon's chorus when a cry of "The trial's beginning!" was heard in the distance.

Secret:
- None stated.

Speech:
- Deep, hollow tone; speaks with a suddenly dropped voice at the end of the first figure.
- Angry when mocked; sighs often.
- Tone of great relief when Alice says her school had no washing.
- Sighs when speaking of not affording extras and of not going to the Classics master.
- Says "Once... I was a real Turtle."
- Dances solemnly round and round Alice, waving forepaws to mark the time.
- Sits on one side of Alice while listening.

entities.name: Gryphon
entities.description:
A Gryphon, a fabulous creature of the sea-shore and Alice's guide through the Mock Turtle's story. Found lying fast asleep in the sun; sits up, rubs its eyes, and chuckles after the Queen leaves. Did not quite like to be looked at. Illustrated in a picture referenced in the text.

Personality:
- Lively, excitable, and impatient; interrupts often, shouts and screams, jumps about wildly, and bounds into the air.
- Decided in tone and rather impatient; repeats its demands.
- Calls the Mock Turtle "old fellow."
- Rather offended at times ("Hm! No accounting for tastes!").
- Dances solemnly round and round Alice, treading on her toes when they pass too close, and waves forepaws to mark the time.
- Speaks in a deep voice at times.
- Hastily dismisses questions it cannot answer.
- Tells Alice she ought to be ashamed of herself for asking such a simple question.
- Tells Alice to hold her tongue before she can speak again.
- Calls Alice a simpleton if she doesn't know what "uglify" is.
- Chuckles and is amused by the Queen's fancies.
- Sighs in its turn when the Mock Turtle recalls Laughing and Grief.
- Took Alice by the hand and hurried her off without waiting for the end of the song.

Wants:
- Wants the Mock Turtle to tell Alice something about the games now.
- Wants the Mock Turtle to drive on, old fellow, and not be all day about it.
- Wants Alice to go on with the next verse, which begins "I passed by his garden."
- Wants to hear Alice's adventures: "Come, let's hear some of your adventures." / "The adventures first."
- Wants the Mock Turtle to sing "Turtle Soup" or to have another figure of the Lobster Quadrille tried.
- Wants Alice to stand up and repeat "'Tis the voice of the sluggard."

Knows:
- The Queen's executions are all her fancy: they never execute nobody, you know.
- The Mock Turtle's sorrow is all his fancy: he hasn't got no sorrow, you know. Come on!
- Introduces Alice as "This here young lady... she wants for to know your history, she do."
- Says "Come on!" repeatedly.
- Says "Chorus again!" and "Come on!"
- Lessons are called lessons "because they lessen from day to day."
- Went to the Classics master, who was an old crab.
- Says "Hadn't time" about never learning Drawling.
- The Quadrille begins with forming a line along the sea-shore.
- The dancers advance twice each with a lobster as a partner, change lobsters, and retire in same order.
- Throw the lobsters as far out to sea as you can, then swim after them, and change lobsters again.
- Clearing the jelly-fish out of the way generally takes some time.
- Whiting have their tails in their mouths because they would go with the lobsters to the dance, so they got thrown out to sea, had to fall a long way, got their tails fast in their mouths, and couldn't get them out again.
- Offers to tell more about why the whiting is called a whiting.
- "It does the boots and shoes."
- Boots and shoes under the sea are done with a whiting.
- Boots and shoes are made of soles and eels, and any shrimp could have told you that.
- Story is "as curious as it can be."
- Verse is different from what he used to say when he was a child.
- The jurors are putting down their names for fear they should forget them before the end of the trial.
- Only answered "Come on!" when Alice asked about the trial.
- Sang the melancholy song "Soo—oop of the e—e—evening, Beautiful, beautiful Soup!" as they fled.
- Lets out a shriek in the sister's dream; the shriek would change to the confused clamour of the farm-yard upon waking.

Secret:
- Tells Alice the Queen's executions are only her fancy, not real.

Speech:
- Speaks half to itself and half to Alice.
- Frequently says "Come on!" and "you know."
- Impatient, clipped phrasing: "The adventures first," "Soles and eels, of course," "Hm! No accounting for tastes!"
- Dialect-heavy speech: "they never executes nobody," "he hasn't got no sorrow," "This here young lady... she wants for to know your history, she do."
- Makes the exclamation "Hjckrrh!" during the Mock Turtle's long silence.
- Lifts both paws in surprise, exclaiming "What! Never heard of uglifying!" and asks whether she knows what to beautify is.

entities.name: Mock Turtle Soup
entities.description: Soup made from the Mock Turtle.

entities.name: Tortoise
entities.description: An old Turtle who was the master at the school in the sea attended by the Mock Turtle. Was nicknamed 'Tortoise' by the Mock Turtle and his classmates because he taught them.

entities.name: ledge of rock
entities.description: A little ledge of rock in the distance, where the Mock Turtle sits sad and lonely.

entities.name: school in the sea
entities.description: The Mock Turtle went to a school where the master was an old Turtle called Tortoise. He and the Gryphon attended this school. The Mock Turtle says they had the best education there and went every day.

entities.name: bottom of the sea
entities.description: Place where the Mock Turtle and the Gryphon live, according to Alice's remark about living there.

entities.name: day-school
entities.description: School Alice says she attended, where she learned French and music.

entities.name: Reeling and Writhing
entities.description: The first part of the regular course at the Mock Turtle's school.

entities.name: Arithmetic
entities.description: Branch of study in the regular course at the Mock Turtle's school, consisting of Ambition, Distraction, Uglification, and Derision.

entities.name: Uglification
entities.description: A branch of Arithmetic at the Mock Turtle's school; Alice has never heard of it. The Gryphon asks whether she knows what to beautify is, implying uglifying is the opposite.

entities.name: French
entities.description: Subject Alice says she learned at her day-school.

entities.name: music
entities.description: Subject Alice says she learned at her day-school.

entities.name: washing
entities.description: Extra subject listed at the Mock Turtle's school as 'French, music, and washing—extra'; Alice says she was not taught it.

entities.name: Drawling-master
entities.description: An old conger-eel that used to come once a week. Taught Drawling, Stretching, and Fainting in Coils.

entities.name: Classics master
entities.description: An old crab. Taught Laughing and Grief. The Gryphon went to him.

entities.name: Mystery
entities.description: Subject taught to the Mock Turtle, described as ancient and modern, taught together with Seaography.

entities.name: Seaography
entities.description: Subject taught to the Mock Turtle together with Mystery.

entities.name: Drawling
entities.description: Subject taught by the Drawling-master to the Mock Turtle. The Mock Turtle cannot show it because he is too stiff.

entities.name: Stretching
entities.description: Subject taught by the Drawling-master to the Mock Turtle.

entities.name: Fainting in Coils
entities.description: Subject taught by the Drawling-master to the Mock Turtle.

entities.name: Laughing and Grief
entities.description: Subjects taught by the Classics master, as the Mock Turtle says they used to say.

entities.name: Lobster Quadrille
entities.description:
The Lobster Quadrille is a dance. It is described as delightful. Dancers form two lines along the sea-shore with seals, turtles, and salmon. They clear away the jelly-fish and advance twice with a lobster as a partner. Then they set to partners and change lobsters. Next, they retire in the same order and throw the lobsters as far out to sea as they can. They swim after them and turn a somersault in the sea. They change lobsters again and return to land, which completes the first figure.

Alice's head is full of the dance as she repeats the verse. The Gryphon mentions the dance and suggests trying another figure of it.

entities.name: sea-shore
entities.description: The place along which dancers first form into a line for the Lobster Quadrille.

entities.name: jelly-fish
entities.description: Must be cleared out of the way before advancing in the Lobster Quadrille; this generally takes some time.

entities.name: lobster
entities.description:
Lobster, a character in the Lobster Quadrille verse and song, who dances with a partner in the quadrille. He trims his belt and buttons and turns out his toes, with his nose.

Personality:
- Advances eagerly when the dance begins.
- Gay as a lark when the sands are dry.
- Timid and tremulous when the tide rises and sharks are around.

Knows:
- Each dancer has one lobster as a partner in the Lobster Quadrille.
- Lobsters are changed, thrown as far out to sea as you can, and swum after.
- Lobsters are waiting on the shingle to join the dance.
- Lobsters will be taken up, thrown, and sent out to sea with the turtles.
- The whiting would go with the lobsters to the dance.
- The Mock Turtle says 'We can do without lobsters.'

Speech:
- Declares 'You have baked me too brown, I must sugar my hair.'
- Talks in contemptuous tones of the Shark when the sands are dry.
- Has a timid and tremulous voice when sharks are around.

entities.name: seals, turtles, salmon
entities.description: Named as the participants forming the two lines in the Lobster Quadrille.

entities.name: whiting
entities.description:
A whiting, a fish that appears in the Mock Turtle's song and in Alice's conversation.

Knows:
- Asks a snail 'Will you walk a little faster?'
- Is mentioned in the Mock Turtle's song, and is the subject of the curious song Alice likes.
- Is said to have been seen by Alice ('you've seen them, of course?').
- Has its tail in its mouth because it would go with the lobsters to the dance and was thrown out to sea, had to fall a long way, and got its tail fast in its mouth.
- Is called a whiting because it does the boots and shoes under the sea.
- Is often seen at dinner by Alice, according to her.
- Would all be washed off crumbs in the sea, per the Mock Turtle, meaning crumbs do not stay on them.
- Is mentioned in conversation: Alice says that if she had been the whiting, she would have told the porpoise to keep back.

Speech:
- 'Will you walk a little faster?'

entities.name: snail
entities.description: Addressed by a whiting to walk faster. Replies 'Too far, too far!' and gives a look askance. Thanks the whiting kindly but will not join the dance; would not, could not join the dance. Is called 'beloved snail' by his scaly friend, who urges him to come and join the dance.

entities.name: porpoise
entities.description:
Porpoise (a fish character from Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, mentioned but not seen directly)

Knows:
- Is mentioned in the song as being close behind the whiting and snail, treading on the whiting's tail.
- Is mentioned in conversation, where Alice tells the whiting to keep back from the porpoise.
- The Mock Turtle says no wise fish would go anywhere without a porpoise.

entities.name: turtles
entities.description: Mentioned in the song: advance eagerly and are waiting on the shingle to join the dance. Will be taken up, thrown, and sent out to sea with the lobsters.

entities.name: scaly friend
entities.description: Friend of the snail, who replies 'What matters it how far we go?' and urges the snail to come and join the dance, saying there is another shore upon the other side. Named only as the snail's 'scaly friend' in the text.

entities.name: dance
entities.description:
A pretty dance is performed. The Gryphon and Mock Turtle dance solemnly around Alice, and the Mock Turtle sings. The first figure is about to be tried. Alice finds the dance interesting to watch and is glad when it ends.

The whiting joins the lobsters in an event. As a result, the lobsters are thrown out to sea.

entities.name: song about the whiting
entities.description: Sung by the Mock Turtle very slowly and sadly. Contains the lines 'Will you walk a little faster?' said a whiting to a snail, and the refrain 'Will you, won't you, will you join the dance?' Alice describes it as curious.

entities.name: shingle
entities.description: A place where the lobsters and turtles are waiting to join the dance.

entities.name: another shore
entities.description: Described by the scaly friend as lying upon the other side, which is not far from France.

entities.name: England
entities.description: Mentioned in the song: the further off from England, the nearer to France.

entities.name: France
entities.description: Mentioned in the song: the further off from England, the nearer to France.

entities.name: boots and shoes
entities.description: Items done with a whiting under the sea, according to the Gryphon. Made of soles and eels, per the Gryphon. Alice's shoes are done with blacking, per Alice's belief.

entities.name: blacking
entities.description: Substance Alice believes her shoes are done with, which makes them shiny.

entities.name: soles
entities.description: Named by the Gryphon as one of the materials boots and shoes are made of.

entities.name: eels
entities.description: Named by the Gryphon as one of the materials boots and shoes are made of.

entities.name: shrimp
entities.description: Mentioned by the Gryphon as one who could have told Alice about the materials of boots and shoes.

entities.name: song
entities.description: The song that was running through Alice's thoughts.

entities.name: 'Tis the voice of the sluggard
entities.description: A lesson verse. The Gryphon tells Alice to stand up and repeat it.

entities.name: Lobster verse
entities.description: Verse Alice recites, with queer words: 'Tis the voice of the Lobster; I heard him declare, 'You have baked me too brown, I must sugar my hair.' As a duck with its eyelids, so he with his nose Trims his belt and his buttons, and turns out his toes. Later editions continue: When the sands are all dry, he is gay as a lark, And will talk in contemptuous tones of the Shark, But, when the tide rises and sharks are around, His voice has a timid and tremulous sound.

entities.name: Shark
entities.description: Mentioned in the verse. The Lobster talks in contemptuous tones of the Shark when the sands are dry. Sharks are around when the tide rises.

entities.name: Owl
entities.description: Character in the poem 'I passed by his garden' who shares a pie with the Panther. Was kindly permitted to pocket the spoon as a boon when the pie was finished.

entities.name: Panther
entities.description: Character in the poem 'I passed by his garden' who shares a pie with the Owl. Took pie-crust, gravy, and meat, and received knife and fork with a growl, concluding the banquet.

entities.name: Turtle Soup
entities.description: Song sung by the Mock Turtle, with the verses beginning 'Beautiful Soup, so rich and green' and 'Beautiful Soup! Who cares for fish'. Its refrain includes 'Soup of the evening, beautiful Soup!'

entities.name: Beautiful Soup
entities.description: Song refrain sung by the Mock Turtle: 'Beautiful Soup, so rich and green, Waiting in a hot tureen! Who for such dainties would not stoop? Soup of the evening, beautiful Soup!' and 'Beautiful Soup! Who cares for fish, Game, or any other dish?'

entities.name: King of Hearts
entities.description: Seated on the throne with the Queen of Hearts when Alice arrived. Was the judge of the trial. Wore his crown over the wig, which made him look uncomfortable and was not becoming.

entities.name: pack of cards
entities.description: A pack of cards gathers in the crowd at the court. They rise into the air and fly down at Alice. This happens when she calls them "nothing but a pack of cards!"

entities.name: little birds and beasts
entities.description: All sorts of little birds and beasts assembled in the crowd about the King and Queen of Hearts.

entities.name: court of justice
entities.description: Court where the trial takes place, with a great crowd assembled, a throne, and a table with a large dish of tarts in the middle.

entities.name: throne
entities.description: Seat on which the King and Queen of Hearts were seated when Alice arrived.

entities.name: dish of tarts
entities.description: Large dish of tarts on the table in the middle of the court; they looked so good that they made Alice quite hungry.

entities.name: trumpet
entities.description: The White Rabbit holds an instrument in one hand. He blows three blasts on it.

entities.name: scroll of parchment
entities.description: Held in the other hand of the White Rabbit.

entities.name: chains
entities.description: Worn by the Knave while he stands before the King and Queen of Hearts.

entities.name: wig
entities.description: Great wig worn by the judge (the King of Hearts); Alice thought the judge was identified by it.

entities.name: crown
entities.description: Worn by the King over the wig, making him look uncomfortable.

entities.name: trial
entities.description: The trial is about who stole the tarts. It is the Trial of the Knave. At first, it has not yet begun. Alice wishes it would finish so refreshments can be handed round. The King says it cannot proceed until all the jurymen are back in their proper places.

entities.name: jury-box
entities.description:
The jury box holds twelve creatures. Some are animals and some are birds. Alice thinks they are the jurors.

Alice tipped the jury box over with the edge of her skirt. The jurymen must be put back in it. The Lizard was placed in it head downwards.

entities.name: twelve jurors
entities.description: Twelve creatures (some animals, some birds) seated in the jury-box, all writing very busily on slates. They are writing down their names for fear they should forget them before the end of the trial, and are writing 'stupid things!' on their slates.

entities.name: squeaking pencil
entities.description: Pencil belonging to one of the jurors (Bill, the Lizard), which squeaked; taken away by Alice.

entities.name: slates
entities.description:
Jurors wrote on slates.
Slates recorded three dates.
Slates recorded "important" or "unimportant."
Slates recorded "She doesn't believe there's an atom of meaning in it."
Bill wrote with one finger on a slate that made no mark.

entities.name: parchment scroll
entities.description: The White Rabbit unrolled an accusation scroll and read it aloud.

entities.name: blowing three blasts on the trumpet
entities.description: The White Rabbit blows three blasts on the trumpet before reading the accusation.

entities.name: jury
entities.description:
This describes the jury in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. Summary:

The jury is told to consider a verdict. They write on slates. One juror adds three dates and converts the total to shillings and pence, and another notes that the Hatter's hat was stolen. One asks what the Dormouse said. Some jurors write "important" and others "unimportant." One asks to whom the letter is addressed. The jury looks puzzled that the verses are not in the prisoner's handwriting, then brightens when the King suggests he imitated someone else's hand. They write that Alice doesn't believe there is an atom of meaning in the paper, but none of them tries to explain it. The King repeatedly tells them to consider their verdict.

entities.name: teacup
entities.description: The Hatter carries a teacup in one hand. In his confusion, he bites a large piece out of it. He later drops the cup. The teacup is also linked to a rattle used during the March Hare's never-ending meal. In reality, the rattle changes into tinkling sheep-bells.

entities.name: piece of bread-and-butter

entities.name: court
entities.description:
This is a summary of descriptions of the court in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.

The court is where the trial takes place. The March Hare, Dormouse, and Hatter all enter it. The King, Queen, Dormouse, Alice, Hatter, and officers are present there. Alice considers leaving. The Dormouse crosses to its other side. The Hatter leaves without putting on his shoes. Sneezing people stand near its door. Confusion starts when the Dormouse is turned out. The Lizard gazes at its roof. The King looks round with a smile. Everybody laughs at the King's pun after a dead silence. Nobody moves when the Queen orders "Off with her head!"

entities.name: verses
entities.description:
Unsigned, unaddressed verses. Not a letter. Nothing written on the outside. Not in the prisoner's handwriting. The White Rabbit reads them aloud.

The verses include these lines:
- "They told me you had been to her, / And mentioned me to him."
- "She gave me a good character, / But said I could not swim."
- "He sent them word I had not gone (We know it to be true)."
- "If she should push the matter on, / What would become of you?"
- "I gave her one, they gave him two, / You gave us three or more."
- "They all returned from him to you, / Though they were mine before."
- "If I or she should chance to be / Involved in this affair."
- "He trusts to you to set them free, / Exactly as we were."
- "Don't let him know she liked them best."
- "before she had this fit."

The King spreads the paper on his knee and thinks it has some meaning. Alice thinks it has no meaning. Nobody explains them.

entities.name: curious dream
entities.description: Alice's dream of her strange Adventures, which she tells to her sister; her sister says it was a curious dream, and Alice thinks it had been a wonderful dream.

entities.name: sister
entities.description: Sits still, leaning her head on her hand, watching the setting sun, thinking of little Alice and all her wonderful Adventures, until she begins dreaming after a fashion. Dreams of little Alice and hears the tones of her voice and sees her queer little toss of her head to keep back the wandering hair that would always get into her eyes. Half believes herself in Wonderland but knows she has only to open her eyes for everything to change to dull reality.

entities.name: Wonderland
entities.description:
Alice's dream is a land of strange creatures. Her sister half believes she is there.
Years later, the sister dreams of Wonderland. She imagines Alice's story being told to other children.

entities.name: setting sun
entities.description: The sun the sister watches while sitting still at the start of the dream.

entities.name: farm-yard
entities.description: The busy farm-yard whose confused clamour the queer noises of the dream would change to upon waking.

entities.name: pig-baby
entities.description: A baby that sneezes on the Duchess's knee while plates and dishes crash around it.

entities.name: shepherd boy
entities.description: In reality, the voice that the Queen's shrill cries would change to upon waking.

entities.name: sheep-bells
entities.description: Tinkling bells that the rattling teacups would change to upon waking from the dream.

entities.name: cattle
entities.description: Their lowing in the distance would take the place of the Mock Turtle's heavy sobs upon waking.

entities.name: little sister
entities.description: The narrator's younger sister. In the after-time she would be a grown woman who keeps the simple and loving heart of her childhood through her riper years. She would gather about her other little children and make their eyes bright and eager with many a strange tale, perhaps even with the dream of Wonderland of long ago. She would feel with all their simple sorrows and find a pleasure in all their simple joys, remembering her own child-life and the happy summer days.

entities.name: other little children
entities.description: Children gathered about the little sister in the after-time. They have simple sorrows and simple joys, and they listen eagerly to strange tales told by her.

entities.name: happy summer days
entities.description: The happy summer days of the little sister's own child-life, which she remembers while sympathizing with other children.
